stocks.m: Identification labels and safety signage; tiny ticket, high switching friction.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual DPS exists for only two years (CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid, 364-day durations: FY2013 0.76, FY2014 0.78) and is used verbatim for those years. No usable quarterly rate series exists (the only quarterly fact is a single 0.20 for Q1 FY2014), so every other year is derived as PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock/PaymentsOfDividends divided by WeightedAverageNumberOfSharesOutstandingBasic for the same FYE (basis 'derived-from-cash'). The derived method is validated against the two filed years: derived/filed = +0.59% (FY2013) and +0.08% (FY2014), both well inside 5%, and FY2026 derived 0.9758 sits -0.43% from the FMP TTM dividend of 0.98. No split adjustment was applied to any year.

specials.note: No special dividends detected. splitFacts is empty and there is no year where a filed DPS sits far above divPaid/sharesBasic; the derived DPS series rises ~2%/yr with no spike. live.regularDividendIfSpecial is null and live.ttmDividend (0.98) matches the FY2026 derived regular rate (0.9758) within 0.5%, so the TTM figure contains no special.

issues: DPS basis is mixed by necessity: only FY2013 (0.76) and FY2014 (0.78) have a filed ~1-year DPS fact (CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid); all 16 other years are divPaid/weighted-basic-shares. Judgement call: filed values kept for 2013-2014 even though derived values there are 0.7645 and 0.7806, so the series carries a small (<0.6%) discontinuity at those two years. All CAGR endpoints (FY2009, FY2016, FY2021, FY2023, FY2026) are on the derived basis, so growth figures are internally consistent.

Cross-check of derived vs filed: FY2013 derived is +0.59% above filed, FY2014 +0.08%. Both inside the 5% tolerance, but the consistent upward bias suggests dividend-bearing shares outstanding (Brady has Class A and Class B common) slightly exceed weighted-average basic shares, so every derived year is likely overstated by roughly 0.1-0.6%. FY2026 derived 0.9758 vs FMP ttmDividend 0.98 (-0.43%) is consistent with that bias.

No split adjustment made to any year; splitAdjustments is empty. splitFacts is empty, sharesBasic falls smoothly from 52.56M (FY2009) to 47.29M (FY2026) (-10% over 17 years) with no step change, and divPaid/sharesBasic is smooth and monotone throughout. Zero fiscal years were divided or multiplied.

Revenue is null for FY2009-FY2018: the primary revenue tag (RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax) starts FY2019 and the Revenues alternative (FY2017-FY2021) is not in the per-year join table. fcfMargin is only computable from FY2019 on.

Net debt is null for FY2009 (no debt tags) and for FY2020-FY2026 (primary debtLT tag LongTermDebtNoncurrent stops at FY2019; the LongTermDebt alternative is not in the join table). Not reported as zero: FY2026 shows PaymentsOfDebtIssuanceCosts of 12.5M, implying borrowings the extraction does not capture. netDebtToEbitda is consequently null for those years, including latest.

ROIC for FY2020-FY2026 uses invested capital = equity - cash with no debt component (debt tags unavailable, treated as zero per the formula). If Brady carried debt in FY2025-FY2026, ROIC for those years is overstated.

Equity is exactly 700,140,000 in FY2017, FY2018 AND FY2019 - almost certainly a stale repeated fact rather than three identical balances. ROIC for FY2018 (0.1601) and especially FY2019 (0.2748) is unreliable and probably overstated.

debtCur is negative in the source for FY2013 (-61,264,000) and FY2014 (-42,514,000), impossible for a balance. Judgement call: absolute values used in netDebt and invested capital for those two years. Also debtCur is identical (61,264,000) in FY2010, FY2011 and FY2012 - another likely repeated fact.

EBITDA is negative in FY2013 (-33.8M; opIncome -82.6M, the goodwill-impairment year) and near zero in FY2014 (3.4M). netDebtToEbitda for those years computes to -5.07x and 35.42x, which is arithmetic but not meaningful, so it is returned as null.

payoutNi is null for FY2012, FY2013 and FY2014 because NetIncomeLoss is negative (-17.9M, -154.5M, -46.0M); these years carry impairment/discontinued-operations effects, visible in FY2012 where pretax 140.7M less tax 37.2M does not reconcile to net income -17.9M. FY2015 payoutNi of 13.72x is real (net income only 3.0M) and is retained.

Effective tax rate not derivable for FY2024-FY2026 (primary pretax tag stops at FY2023, alternative not in the join table); the 21% fallback was used for ROIC there. FY2013's implied rate (42.6M tax on a -95.7M pretax loss = -44.5%) was rejected as out of range and the 21% fallback applied. FY2015 (80.4%) and FY2018 (40.1%, tax-reform year) were unusual but in range and used as filed.

Streak is window-limited: data starts at FY2009 and every year FY2010-FY2026 is a strict increase (17 in a row), with no cut or hold. The true streak very likely extends before FY2009 (priorEstimates guessed 40 years) but that is not derivable here. FY2020 and FY2021 both increased, so cut2020 is false.
fcfGrowth5 (FY2021 to FY2026, 1.54%/yr) is noisy: FCF swings from 75.3M (FY2022) to 189.9M (FY2023) and capex spikes to 79.9M in FY2024, so the endpoint CAGR understates the underlying trend.
priorEstimates (growth5y 3%, streak 40, payoutPctFcf 30%) were not used. Measured: g5 2.11%/yr, 17 increases visible in data, latest FCF payout 23.95%.

normalised.notes: Brady Corp (CIK 0000746598), FYE July 31, so FY2026 = year ended 2026-07-31. Regular DPS rises in every year of the window, 0.6819 (FY2009) to 0.9758 (FY2026), a steady ~2%/yr grind with no cuts, holds or specials. Cover is comfortable and improving: FCF payout 23.9% and NI payout 22.5% in FY2026 versus a 35-40% norm earlier in the window (the FY2014 spike to 80.9% reflects the impairment-era cash-flow trough, not a dividend change). Share count is down ~10% since FY2009 on steady buybacks (42.2M repurchased in FY2026), so cash dividends paid grew far more slowly (35.8M to 46.1M) than DPS. No split occurred in this window and no year's share basis was altered. Main data gaps: balance-sheet debt from FY2020 onward (so leverage is null for the latest year) and revenue before FY2019.

Internal-consistency probes on source data: FY2012 pretax 140655 less tax 37162 = 103493 does not reconcile to NetIncomeLoss -17911 (discontinued ops); equity is byte-identical 700140000 in FY2017/18/19; debtCur is identical 61264000 in FY2010/11/12 and negative in FY2013/14. issues.detail: The null/zero handling for debt is internally inconsistent. For FY2015-FY2017 a missing debtCur was silently treated as zero (netDebt = debtLT - cash), but for FY2020 - where debtCur IS present and equals 0 and only debtLT is missing - netDebt was returned null. Under the same convention FY2020 would be 0 + 0 - 217643000 = -217,643,000. Separately, the evidence that real debt exists from FY2025 is stronger than the record states: InterestExpense rises from 437,000 (FY2021) to 1,276,000, 3,539,000, 3,126,000, 4,747,000 and 9,699,000 (FY2026), a ~20x increase that cannot come from a zero-debt balance sheet, and PaymentsOfDebtIssuanceCosts is 12,500,000 in FY2026. The families block also lists a LongTermDebt alternative with 10 points running to 2026-07-31 that was not pulled into the join table.
issues.suggested: Keep netDebt null for FY2021-FY2026 (not derivable from the table), but either set FY2020 netDebt = -217,643,000 for consistency with the FY2015-FY2017 convention, or restate FY2015-FY2017 as null too. Add an explicit issue: 'InterestExpense grows 437K (FY2021) -> 9,699K (FY2026); the LongTermDebt alternative tag (10 points, last 2026-07-31) was not joined, so latest-year leverage is unknown rather than low.'

issues.detail: ROIC for FY2025-FY2026 uses invested capital = equity - cash with the debt component forced to zero, while FY2026 interest expense of 9,699,000 implies roughly 150-250M of borrowings at plausible rates. The record calls this 'overstated' but does not size it. With ~200M of debt, FY2026 invested capital would be ~1,370,413,000 instead of 1,170,413,000 and ROIC would fall from 0.1779 to ~0.152 - a ~2.6pp overstatement, not a rounding effect.
issues.suggested: Either return roic null for FY2025-FY2026, or keep 0.1837/0.1779 with an explicit magnitude note: 'debt component missing; each 100M of unrecognised debt lowers FY2026 ROIC by ~1.4pp.'

issues.detail: debtCur is -61,264,000 (FY2013) and -42,514,000 (FY2014) in the source - impossible for a balance and almost certainly a sign-flipped extraction. The record takes absolute values and folds them into netDebt and invested capital. That is inventing a sign the source does not support, and it is not a neutral choice: it adds 61.3M to FY2013 invested capital (1,002,153,000 vs 940,889,000), making FY2013 ROIC -0.0651 instead of -0.0693. Note also that 61,264,000 is the exact value repeated in FY2010, FY2011 and FY2012, so FY2013's entry is likely a stale repeated fact rather than a real FY2013 current maturity at all.
issues.suggested: Prefer treating FY2013/FY2014 debtCur as unavailable (null) rather than abs(): FY2013 netDebt = 201150000 - 91058000 = 110,092,000 and FY2014 = 159296000 - 81834000 = 77,462,000, with roic FY2013 -0.0693 and FY2014 -0.0480. At minimum, state that abs() was chosen over null and that it moves ROIC.

issues.detail: yearsCovered is reported as 18 while gMax was computed with N=17 ((0.9758/0.6819)^(1/17)-1 = 2.130%, which I confirm). 18 is the number of data points, not the number of compounding years; a consumer reading yearsCovered as the CAGR horizon would recompute gMax as 2.011% and see a 0.12pp mismatch.
issues.suggested: Set yearsCovered = 17 (FY2009 to FY2026 is 17 compounding years), or rename the field to reflect that it counts data points.

issues.detail: The series deliberately mixes bases at exactly the two years used to validate the derived method, which makes the validation partly circular and injects a real (if small) non-monotonicity in the growth rate: FY2012->FY2013 is +2.48% on the published series but +3.10% on a consistent derived basis, and FY2013->FY2014 is +2.63% published vs +2.10% derived. Since every CAGR endpoint (FY2009/2016/2021/2023/2026) is derived, the two filed values contribute nothing to any reported statistic while breaking basis consistency.
issues.suggested: Either use the derived values throughout for series consistency (FY2013 0.7645, FY2014 0.7806) and keep the filed 0.76/0.78 only as the validation cross-check, or keep the filed values and add a field marking that the FY2012->FY2014 year-over-year changes are basis-contaminated.

issues.detail: The record states revenue is unavailable before FY2019, but families.revenue lists a Revenues alternative with 5 points spanning 2017-07-31 to 2021-07-31. Two of those years (FY2017, FY2018) are genuinely recoverable and were dropped only because the alternative tag was never joined into the table - a pipeline gap, not an absence of data. This is a recoverable-data issue stated as an unrecoverable one.
issues.suggested: Re-run the join including the Revenues alternative to populate FY2017-FY2018 revenue and fcfMargin, or reword the issue to 'the Revenues alternative tag covering FY2017-FY2021 exists in families but was not joined' rather than implying no revenue fact exists.

issues.detail: Confirming and sharpening the record's own flag: StockholdersEquity is byte-identical 700,140,000 in FY2017, FY2018 and FY2019 while assets move 1,050,223,000 -> 1,056,931,000 -> 1,157,308,000 and cumulative net income over FY2018-FY2019 is 222.3M against only 87.6M of dividends and 4.6M of buybacks. Equity mathematically cannot be flat across those years, so FY2019 ROIC of 0.2748 is not merely 'unreliable' - the denominator is demonstrably wrong and the true FY2019 figure is materially lower.
issues.suggested: Return roic null for FY2018 and FY2019 rather than publishing 0.1601 and 0.2748, or flag them with a severity that prevents their use in any trend comparison.

issues.detail: The streak of 17 is arithmetically correct on the published series, but 16 of the 18 points are divPaid/weighted-basic-shares, not declared dividend rates. Because Brady buys back stock every year (share count -10% over the window), the derived series mechanically rises even in a year where the declared rate is held flat: FY2023 divPaid actually FELL (45,931,000 -> 45,404,000) and FY2024 fell again (-> 45,060,000), yet derived DPS rose 0.895 -> 0.9156 -> 0.9364 purely from the shrinking denominator. The streak is therefore not independent evidence of 17 declared-rate increases.
issues.suggested: Add an issue stating: 'divPaid declined in FY2023 (-1.1%) and FY2024 (-0.8%); the derived DPS increases in those years come entirely from a falling share count, so the 17-year increase streak is a property of the derivation and is not corroborated by filed rate facts.' Consider lowering confidence on the streak field specifically.

issues.detail: The 17-increase streak is inferred almost entirely from a derived divPaid/weighted-basic-shares series, which mechanically rises whenever the share count falls even if the per-share rate were held flat. FY2024 is the clearest case: cash dividends paid actually FELL (45,404k -> 45,060k) yet derived DPS rose 0.9156 -> 0.9364 purely because sharesBasic dropped 49.59M -> 48.12M. The conclusion happens to be right for Brady (a genuine multi-decade raiser, and live ttmDividend corroborates the FY2026 level), but the derived basis cannot by itself evidence 'strict increase' in any single year. Not blocking: the record already discloses the mixed basis and windowLimited=true.
issues.suggested: Keep consecutiveIncreasesInData=17 and windowLimited=true, but add to dataQuality: 'Increases in derived years are share-count sensitive - e.g. FY2024 divPaid fell 0.8% while derived DPS rose 2.3% on a 3.0% lower share count - so the streak is corroborative rather than directly filed evidence.'

issues.detail: External-coherence gap rather than an error: netDebt/netDebtToEbitda are null for FY2020-FY2026 because LongTermDebtNoncurrent stops at FY2019, yet the source file shows a LongTermDebt alternative with 10 points running first 2010-07-31 to last 2026-07-31 that would cover exactly the missing years. The record's own note says the alternative 'is not in the join table', so the null is a pipeline limitation, not an absence of debt - and FY2026 PaymentsOfDebtIssuanceCosts of 12.5M implies real borrowings. Leverage for the latest year is therefore unknown, not zero, and ROIC FY2020-FY2026 (including latest 0.1779) is overstated to the extent debt exists.
issues.suggested: Keep the nulls (do not report 0.0x), but promote this to a visible caveat on 'latest': netDebtToEbitda unavailable because the LongTermDebt fallback tag (10 points, FY2010-FY2026) was not joined; re-run the extraction with LongTermDebt as the debtLT fallback to populate FY2020-FY2026 leverage and correct ROIC.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: 5-yr DPS CAGR FY2021 0.8791 -> FY2026 0.9758 = 2.109%/yr; g3 2.145%, g10 1.912%, gMax 2.130%. A cost-of-living raise, not compounding.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: FY2026 dividends 46,139,000 / FCF 192,654,000 = 23.95%; NI payout 22.47%. Just inside the band and the most comfortable cover in the whole 18-year window (35-40% was the earlier norm).

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to still be fast
rules.note: Every year FY2010-FY2026 is a strict increase, and the streak runs to the start of the XBRL window (FY2009), so it is window-limited. The prior research figure of ~40 years is plausible for Brady and is used; at 40 years the policy is proven but the company is long past the fast phase, so the rule fails on the upper bound.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF endpoints are erratic - 178.5M (FY2021), 75.3M (FY2022), 189.9M (FY2023), 175.2M (FY2024 on a 79.9M capex spike), 153.6M (FY2025), 192.7M (FY2026) - so per the rule net income is used: 129,659,000 -> 205,378,000 = 9.64%/yr, comfortably above the 2.11% dividend growth. On the raw FCF endpoints the measure would fail by 0.57pp.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2026 ROIC 17.79% on invested capital = equity - cash, with the debt component missing from the extraction. FY2026 interest expense of 9,699,000 implies roughly $200M of borrowings; adding that would cut ROIC to about 15.2%. Passes either way, and the FY2023-FY2026 range of 17.8%-23.6% is consistently high.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: netDebt/EBITDA is null FY2020-FY2026 because the LongTermDebt fallback tag was never joined - this is a pipeline gap, not evidence of zero debt. Brady was net cash through FY2019 (-228.9M) and the largest leverage in the whole window was 1.15x (FY2015); even the ~$200M implied by FY2026 interest expense is ~0.65x against $308.4M EBITDA. Passing on that bound, but the latest-year figure is genuinely unverified.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: Identification labels, wire markers and safety signage are low-ticket consumables specified into customer workflows, printers and compliance documentation, so requalifying a rival to save a few dollars per order is not worth the switching friction - 11.6% FCF margin and 17.8% ROIC on a $1.66B revenue base confirm it is not price competition.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/2021; no cut anywhere in window
rules.value: no cut; raised through FY2020 and FY2021
rules.note: DPS rose 0.8505 -> 0.8672 (FY2020) -> 0.8791 (FY2021) and in every other year of the window; no cut, no hold, no suspension FY2009-FY2026. 2008 sits outside the XBRL window and is not assessable here. Caveat: 16 of 18 years are derived from cash dividends / share count, and divPaid actually fell in FY2023 (-1.1%) and FY2024 (-0.8%) while buybacks shrank the share count, so the derived increases in those years are share-count sensitive rather than filed-rate evidence.

analysis.assessment: Brady is a high-quality, cheap-to-own industrial compounder that is a poor dividend-growth engine at today's price: a 1.15% starting yield (0.9758 DPS on an $84.60 share) growing at 2.11%/yr over five years means the income never compounds into anything - after a decade the yield on cost is still under 1.5%. Everything defensive is in order: FY2026 dividends of $46.1M take only 23.9% of $192.7M FCF and 22.5% of net income, ROIC is 17.8% (about 15% once the roughly $200M of borrowings implied by $9.7M of interest expense is added back), leverage is well under 1x on any reasonable reconstruction, and the payout has risen in all 17 years visible since FY2009 on a streak that almost certainly runs ~40 years. Earnings are outgrowing the dividend by a wide margin - net income compounded 9.6%/yr from FY2021 to FY2026 against 2.1% dividend growth - which is the tell: management is deliberately routing cash to buybacks (share count down 10% to 47.3M) rather than to raises. The thing most likely to break the thesis is not the dividend, which is nearly unbreakable at this cover, but the owner's patience: at a sub-25% payout and 2%/yr raises the snowball simply never gets large, and the policy has been stable for long enough that a re-acceleration is unlikely. Worth flagging that latest-year leverage is genuinely unverified - the LongTermDebt tag was never joined - so the balance-sheet pass rests on inference rather than a filed figure.

normalised.dpsMethod: Rule (a) for FY2009-FY2025; Rule (b) for FY2026. FY2009-FY2011 and FY2014-FY2025 come from the filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid fact (364-365 day, start 07-01, end 06-30, 10-K). FY2012 and FY2013 have no CashPaid FY-duration fact and were filled from the filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared fact (0.80 and 0.88, 364-365 day 10-K durations); the two tags agree to the cent on all four overlapping years (FY2010 0.60, FY2011 0.70, FY2014 0.96, FY2015 1.04), so the splice needs no re-basing. FY2026 is the exception: the filed annual CashPaid fact of 1.99 was REJECTED and replaced by the sum of quarterly rates 0.46+0.46+0.51+0.51 = 1.94. Reason, from the raw facts: for every fiscal year FY2010-FY2025 except FY2011 the annual CashPaid fact equals exactly 2*Q1rate + 2*Q3rate, i.e. one rate step per fiscal year with Q4 = Q3 (verified arithmetically for all 15 of those years); FY2011 is the only variant and it is still a single step, taken in Q4 instead of Q3. AIT has never taken two rate steps in one fiscal year in 17 years of quarterly facts. The filed 1.99 requires Jul-Sep 2025 = 0.46, Oct-Dec 2025 = 0.46 (filed), Jan-Mar 2026 = 0.51 (filed) and Apr-Jun 2026 = 0.56, i.e. a second step three months after the January step. Jul-Sep 2025 = 0.46 is not an assumption - it is forced, being sandwiched between the FY2025 back-half rate of 0.46 and the filed Oct-Dec 2025 fact of 0.46. That leaves Apr-Jun 2026 as the only free quarter, and cash settles it: divPaid/sharesBasic = 72,598k/37,377k = 1.94232, which is +0.119% against 1.94 - squarely inside the +0.02% to +0.55% band this ratio occupies in all 17 other years - and -2.40% against 1.99, a sign flip four times larger than any other year. FY2026 basis is therefore 'summed-quarters'. Every year was cross-checked against divPaid/sharesBasic; on the corrected series all 18 years agree within 0.56% and every sign is positive.

specials.note: No special dividends. splitFacts is empty and no special-dividend fact appears anywhere in dpsAllFacts. The decisive test is that regular DPS never sits materially above divPaid/sharesBasic: on the corrected series the cash-per-share ratio sits ABOVE reported DPS in all 18 years by +0.02% to +0.55% (ordinary intra-year share-count drift plus dividends paid on unvested restricted shares), with FY2026 at +0.12%. There is no year where DPS exceeds cash paid, which is the signature a special would leave. live.regularDividendIfSpecial is null. live.ttmDividend is 1.99 as of 2026-09-17, but note that the TTM window is calendar-aligned (roughly Oct 2025 - Sep 2026 on a declared basis), not fiscal-aligned: under the single-January-raise reading it sums to 0.46+0.51+0.51+0.51 = 1.99 while the fiscal year Jul 2025 - Jun 2026 sums to 0.46+0.46+0.51+0.51 = 1.94. The TTM figure is therefore consistent with, and in fact explains, the 1.94 fiscal-year total; it is supportive context, not independent confirmation of any fiscal-year number. AIT's dividend tag is 'CashPaid' and the declared-basis tag agrees with it on all overlapping years, so there is no declared-vs-paid timing artefact to mistake for a special.

They are the only two years where the dividend consumed more than half of free cash flow.

RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY on FY2026 DPS. The restatement to 1.94 contradicts an explicit filed 10-K annual fact, which is not done lightly. It should be confirmed against the FY2026 10-K dividend note or the Apr-Jun 2026 quarterly rate once filed. If the 10-K text genuinely states 1.99 of dividends paid per share for the fiscal year, then either divPaid of 72,598k or sharesBasic of 37,377k must be misstated, since 1.99 x 37,377k = 74.4m against a filed 72,598k. Confidence is held at 'medium' rather than 'high' for this reason, alongside the five-year gap in netDebt/netDebtToEbitda/ROIC (FY2022-FY2026, including the latest year) and the eight-year gap in revenue (FY2009-FY2016).

normalised.notes:
AIT is a June-FYE filer. FY2026 ended 2026-06-30 and is complete in the data.

FY2026 DPS: the reviewers' block is upheld and the year is restated from the filed 1.99 to 1.94. The reasoning is rebuilt from the raw facts rather than taken from either the prior record or the review. Two things settle it. First, the quarterly structure: across FY2010-FY2025 the filed annual CashPaid fact equals 2*Q1rate + 2*Q3rate in 15 of 16 testable years, and the sixteenth (FY2011: 0.17/0.17/0.17 with a 0.70 annual, implying a 0.19 Q4) is still a single rate step, merely taken in Q4 rather than Q3. AIT has never taken two steps in one fiscal year. Reaching 1.99 requires exactly that - 0.46 in Jul-Sep 2025 and Oct-Dec 2025, 0.51 from January, then 0.56 from April. Second, cash: divPaid/sharesBasic is 1.94232, which is +0.12% against 1.94 and -2.40% against 1.99. That ratio is positive in all 17 other years and never exceeds +0.55%, so 1.94 sits inside the distribution and 1.99 is the sole sign flip at four times the largest deviation. Jul-Sep 2025 is not a free parameter - it is pinned to 0.46 between the FY2025 back-half rate and the filed Oct-Dec 2025 fact - so Apr-Jun 2026 is the only quarter in dispute, and cash chooses 0.51 over 0.56. The prior record's '0.56' was an invented residual and is deleted, as is its claim that live.ttmDividend corroborates 1.99: 1.99 is precisely what the Oct 2025 - Sep 2026 declared window sums to under a single January raise (0.46 + 0.51 x 3), which supports 1.94 for the fiscal year, not 1.99. The prior record's share-count-timing explanation for the 2.4% gap is also withdrawn - shares fall only 2.4% across the year against a 10.9% back-half rate step, so that effect is worth 0.2-0.5%, not 2.4%, and it cannot discharge the anomaly it was offered for.

Where the reviewers were not followed: both offered the alternative of keeping 1.99 at 'low' confidence. That is not adopted, because the evidence is not merely suggestive - the 2+2 pattern holds in every testable year and the sign of the cash ratio is invariant across 18 years. Equally, reviewer 2's suggestion to surface the cash-is-zero lower-bound ROIC into latest.roic is declined: that figure is not the defined ROIC (net debt is undefined without cash) and putting it in the reported field would conflict with fin[2026].roic being null. It is carried in dataQuality.issues instead, explicitly labelled a lower bound, so a consumer does not read the null as risk. The restatement does override an explicit filed fact, so it is flagged for confirmation against the 10-K dividend note and confidence is held at 'medium'.

FY2010 balance sheet: the reviewer is right and the year is nulled. LongTermDebtNoncurrent is an affirmative filed 0 at 2010-06-30, but the DebtCurrent family lists a point at that date with no value supplied, and interest expense was 5,738k. Treating debtCur as 0 assumed a value for a tag the source shows exists, which is the same situation as FY2009 and FY2011-FY2013 that the record already nulled. netDebt, netDebt/EBITDA and ROIC for FY2010 are now null, with the -175,777k / -1.4465x / 18.21% figures kept in issues as upper-bound references.

Splits: no adjustment to any year, verified three ways - splitFacts is empty, there is no ratio step in sharesBasic, and divPaid/sharesBasic reproduces the DPS series within 0.56% in all 18 years, which cannot happen across a basis break. The prior record's supporting claim that sharesBasic declines monotonically is false (it rises in FY2010, FY2011, FY2021, FY2023 and FY2024) and has been corrected; the conclusion itself is unaffected and splitAdjustments stays empty.

The dividend record is otherwise clean: an unbroken regular series across 18 fiscal years, no specials, no cuts, and one hold (FY2010 flat at 0.60 through the financial crisis). That hold is inside the data window, so the 16-year run of strictly rising DPS from FY2011 through FY2026 is a bounded count, not a window-limited one. 1.66 -> 1.94 is still an increase, so the streak is unaffected by the restatement.

Growth on the corrected series: 5.84% over ten years, 8.34% over five, 12.02% over three. The acceleration comes from FY2025 (+15.3%) and FY2026 (+16.9%), funded by FCF that more than doubled in five years (225.8m to 460.5m, a 15.32% CAGR). FCF payout fell from roughly 30% pre-2020 to 15.76% in FY2026, so the acceleration was paid for by cash generation, not by stretching the payout. FY2026 FCF margin was 9.27% on 4.97bn of revenue.

The main remaining gap is the balance sheet, not the dividend. Cash is unavailable for FY2022-FY2026 because the primary tag stops at FY2021 and the successor restricted-cash tag supplies no values, so netDebt, netDebt/EBITDA and ROIC are null for the five most recent years. Gross debt was not substituted, which would have shown FY2026 net debt of 262.3m for a company holding 257.7m of cash as recently as FY2021.

REPAIR: FY2026 DPS restated 1.99 -> 1.94 (basis 'filed' -> 'summed-quarters') on the one-step-per-year quarterly invariant plus the divPaid/sharesBasic reconciliation (+0.12% vs -2.40%); latest.dps 1.99 -> 1.94; growth g3 12.98 -> 12.02, g5 8.89 -> 8.34, g10 6.11 -> 5.84, gMax 7.31 -> 7.15; the invented FY2026 Q4 rate of 0.56 and the claim that live.ttmDividend corroborates 1.99 both deleted, replaced by the calendar-vs-fiscal-window explanation; the share-count-timing explanation for the FY2026 gap withdrawn as quantitatively insufficient; FY2010 netDebt (-175,777k), netDebtToEbitda (-1.4465) and roic (0.1821) set to null because DebtCurrent has an unvalued point at 2010-06-30, with those figures moved to issues as upper-bound references; the false 'monotonically declining sharesBasic' claim corrected; cross-check table, specials note, dpsMethod and notes rewritten accordingly. Unchanged and independently re-verified: all other fin values, splitAdjustments = [], hasSpecials = false, streak 16, cut2020 false, fcfGrowth5 15.32, confidence 'medium'.

The 0.56 is not a filed fact - it is a residual invented to force the sum to 1.99, and it implies a SECOND rate increase inside FY2026 (0.46 -> 0.51 -> 0.56), which is out of character for AIT's once-a-year January raise cadence. The more natural reconstruction from the two facts that DO exist is 0.46 + 0.46 + 0.51 + 0.51 = 1.940, which reproduces the independent cross-check divPaid/sharesBasic = 72,598/37,377 = 1.9423 to within 0.1% - far better than 1.99's -2.40% miss. That makes the record's 'mid-year raise against a falling share count' explanation for the FY2026 gap weaker than stated, since a single raise with a flat Q4 already explains the cash figure without invoking share-count drift. This does not change the headline (the filed annual 10-K fact and live.ttmDividend both say 1.99, so check 1 passes either way), but the invented 0.56 should not be carried forward as if it were filed.

The filed FY2026 annual CashPaid fact of 1.99 is used as-is.' issues.detail: The note cites 'live.ttmDividend (1.99) equals the filed FY2026 annual DPS exactly' as corroboration that the whole 1.99 is regular. This is weaker corroboration than presented: live.ttmDividend is dated 2026-09-17 and is the sum of the last four DECLARED dividends, i.e. a calendar window roughly Oct 2025 - Sep 2026, not the Jul 2025 - Jun 2026 fiscal year. Under a single-raise reading (0.46 declared Oct 2025, then 0.51 x3) the TTM window also sums to exactly 1.99 while the fiscal year sums to 1.94 - so the agreement is consistent with either reading and cannot by itself confirm the fiscal-year figure. The conclusion that there is no special dividend still stands on the other evidence (regularDividendIfSpecial null, smooth divPaid progression 55.9m -> 63.7m -> 72.6m, no DPS spike).
issues.suggested: Reword to: 'live.regularDividendIfSpecial is null and live.ttmDividend is 1.99; note that the TTM window is calendar-aligned, not fiscal-aligned, so its agreement with the FY2026 annual fact is supportive but not independent confirmation of the fiscal-year total.' Keep hasSpecials=false.

issues.detail: Confidence is 'medium', which the balance-sheet gaps justify, but the label should be read as applying to the FIN block rather than to the dividend series: netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and ROIC are null for the five most recent years (FY2022-FY2026) including the latest, so latest.netDebtToEbitda and latest.roic are both null and no leverage or returns screen can run off this record. Externally this is a live problem, not a cosmetic one: a $11.6bn-cap distributor with $262.3m gross debt and roughly 19.7% lower-bound ROIC is an easy, unlevered dividend payer, and a downstream consumer that reads null as 'unknown/risky' will mis-rank it.

issues.detail: FY2026 DPS of 1.99 is contradicted by three independent pieces of evidence in the raw file, and the record's stated justification for keeping it is itself fabricated. (a) Cash paid per weighted basic share is 72,598/37,377 = 1.9423, i.e. filed DPS sits 2.40% ABOVE cash-per-share. In every one of the other 17 years the ratio sits slightly BELOW... i.e. divPaid/shares is ABOVE filed DPS by +0.02% to +0.55%. FY2026 is the only sign flip and is 4x the largest prior deviation. (b) The quarterly rate facts constrain the year: the rate was 0.46 from Jan-2025 (FY2025 Q3 fact 0.46), the Oct-Dec 2025 fact is 0.46 and the Jan-Mar 2026 fact is 0.51. So Jul-Sep 2025 can only be 0.46, which forces Apr-Jun 2026 = 0.56 to reach 1.99 - a second raise inside six months, against AIT's one-raise-per-January pattern. (c) Decisively, live.ttmDividend = 1.99 as of 2026-09-17 covers the payments of Dec-2025, Mar-2026, Jun-2026 and Sep-2026. 0.46+0.51+0.51+0.51 = 1.99 exactly, which requires Apr-Jun 2026 = 0.51, NOT 0.56. If Q4 were 0.56 the TTM would be 2.09. The live TTM therefore refutes, rather than corroborates, the 1.99 FY2026 total - the record has the logic backwards. A share-weighted reconstruction confirms it: with shares falling ~37.7m to ~36.8m across the year, quarters 0.46/0.46/0.51/0.51 imply ~72.2m of cash paid against the actual 72,598k (0.5% low), while 0.46/0.46/0.51/0.56 implies ~74.1m (2.0% too high). Every line of evidence points to a FY2026 regular total of 1.94; the 1.99 XBRL annual fact looks like a filer/extraction artefact (most plausibly the current TTM/run-rate tagged into the FY context). The record also asserts '0.46+0.46+0.51+0.56 = 1.99 is the consistent quarterly decomposition' - the 0.56 appears nowhere in dpsAllFacts and is an invented number, in direct breach of the 'never invent a number' rule.
issues.suggested: Either set dps[2026].val = 1.94 with basis 'derived' (sum of quarterly rates 0.46+0.46+0.51+0.51, corroborated by divPaid/sharesBasic = 1.9423, a +0.12% gap in line with the FY2009-FY2025 pattern), or keep the filed 1.99 but drop confidence to 'low' and flag the year as unverified. If restated to 1.94: latest.dps = 1.94, growth.g3 = 12.02, g5 = 8.34, g10 = 5.84, gMax = 7.15 (payout ratios, streak=16, cut2020=false and all fin values are unaffected). Delete the fabricated '0.56' quarter and the claim that live.ttmDividend corroborates 1.99 - it does the opposite.

issues.detail: The stated mechanism for the FY2026 gap ('the higher per-share rate applies to fewer shares than the full-year weighted average') is directionally right but quantitatively cannot produce 2.4%. Shares fall only ~3% across FY2026 and the raise is ~11% in the back half; the resulting wedge between sum-of-rates and divPaid/weighted-shares is on the order of 0.2-0.5%, consistent with the FY2009-FY2025 record, not 2.4%. The explanation therefore does not discharge the anomaly it is offered for.
issues.suggested: Replace with: 'FY2026 gap of -2.40% is NOT explained by share-count timing (that effect is worth ~0.3%); it indicates the filed 1.99 annual fact is inconsistent with the quarterly facts and with cash paid.'

Assuming a value for a tag the source shows exists but did not deliver is inventing a number, and it flatters both figures (ROIC denominator too small, net debt too negative).

rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: live marketCap 11,646,308,045 at $315.11 on 2026-09-17. Passes the 15B bar but is well above the 5B ideal, so the base is large enough that incremental M&A moves the needle less than it did a decade ago.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: 1.94 regular annual DPS / 315.11 = 0.616%. On the filed (rejected) 1.99 it would still be only 0.63%. AIT has never been a yield stock; the shares have re-rated to ~28x earnings and ~25x FCF, so almost all of the return has to come from growth and multiple, not from the starting coupon. Fails decisively - not a borderline miss.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: 5-yr DPS CAGR FY2021 1.30 -> FY2026 1.94. Passes but not 'strong'. The recent run is far faster: g3 is 12.02% on the back of +15.3% (FY2025) and +16.9% (FY2026) raises, versus g10 of just 5.84% - the policy changed around FY2025, it did not compound at this rate for a decade.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: FY2026 dividends 72,598k / FCF 460,517k = 15.76%. This fails the rule on the LOW side, which is the benign failure mode: payout on net income is 17.5% and the ratio has fallen from ~30% pre-2020. It means enormous runway (dividends could nearly quadruple on today's FCF before hitting 60%) but also that management is deliberately not returning much - buybacks took $317m in FY2026, roughly 4x the dividend.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy
rules.note: Strictly rising DPS FY2011 through FY2026. Not window-limited: the FY2010 hold (0.60 flat through the crisis) is visible inside the data, so the count is bounded by an observed event rather than by the start of XBRL. priorEstimates.streak of 16 agrees; the data figure is used.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF FY2021 225,845k -> FY2026 460,517k. Cash generation grew almost twice as fast as the dividend, which is exactly why the payout ratio fell while the raises accelerated. Net income corroborates: 144,757k -> 414,525k, a 23.4% CAGR.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: Reported roic is null for FY2022-FY2026 because the cash tag stops at FY2021, so the strict formula cannot be run. The cash-treated-as-zero computation is a LOWER bound (denominator too large) and gives 19.70% for FY2026, 16.18% FY2025, 16.80% FY2024. True ROIC is higher still. Even the bound clears the 15% 'strong' line, so the rule passes on a floor, not on an estimate. FY2017-FY2021 filed ROIC ran 2.6%-15.1%, so the step-up since FY2022 is real and recent.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: Net debt is not derivable for FY2026 (no cash value filed). Gross debt of 262,300k against EBITDA of 575,344k is 0.456x, and that is an UPPER bound since any cash reduces it - AIT held 257,745k of cash as recently as FY2021, which would put it near net cash. Gross debt fell from 572,300k in FY2025 to 262,300k in FY2026. Historical peak leverage was 3.73x in FY2018 (Fluid Power acquisition) and 6.04x in FY2020 on collapsed EBITDA; both were worked down without touching the dividend.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: ~600 service centres and fluid-power/flow-control shops put inventory within hours of the customer's plant; when a bearing or hydraulic assembly fails, downtime cost dwarfs part price, so the buyer pays for availability and technical fitment rather than shopping the price. Switching means re-qualifying a vendor across dozens of sites. Real, but it is a service-density moat, not a patent - a rival with equal local density competes on equal terms, and the 9.3% FCF margin shows distribution economics, not monopoly economics.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.note: FY2019 1.22 -> FY2020 1.26 -> FY2021 1.30, raised in both years despite FY2020 net income collapsing to 24.0m (203% payout on earnings; FCF payout was only 17.7%, which is how it was funded). No cut or suspension anywhere in the 18-year window. 2008 is outside the XBRL window and is not assessed; the FY2010 hold at 0.60 is the closest the record comes, and a hold is not a cut.

analysis.assessment: AIT passes eight of ten rules, but it fails the two that decide whether a dividend-growth snowball can actually start: the yield is 0.62% (1.94 / $315.11) and the FCF payout is 15.8%, below the 20% floor. The business itself is excellent - FCF doubled in five years to $460.5m (15.3% CAGR) against 8.3% dividend growth, ROIC is at least 19.7% even with cash counted as zero, and gross debt of $262.3m is 0.46x EBITDA - so the dividend is the safest line in the record, not the most interesting one. At this payout the dividend could nearly quadruple before reaching 60% of FCF, and the FY2025 (+15.3%) and FY2026 (+16.9%) raises suggest management has started using some of that room, which is why g3 of 12.0% runs far ahead of g10 of 5.84%. What most likely breaks it is not the dividend but the entry price: $11.6bn at ~28x earnings and ~25x FCF on a cyclical MRO distributor means a single industrial destocking cycle (revenue fell 3.4% in FY2020 and EBITDA more than halved) resets the multiple while the 0.6% yield pays you almost nothing to wait. Secondary caution: the FY2026 DPS of 1.94 overrides an explicit filed 10-K fact of 1.99 and the balance sheet has no derivable cash for five straight years, so leverage and ROIC are bounds rather than measurements.
analysis.moat: Industrial parts distribution with ~600 local service centres: same-day availability and technical fitment on parts whose failure shuts a plant down means customers buy proximity, not price, and switching requires re-qualifying a vendor across dozens of sites.
strengths: FCF 5-yr CAGR of 15.32% ($225.8m -> $460.5m) comfortably outruns the 8.34% dividend CAGR - the raises are funded by cash generation, not by stretching the payout.
FY2026 FCF payout of 15.8% and NI payout of 17.5% leave roughly 4x headroom before the 60% ceiling.
Lower-bound FY2026 ROIC of 19.7% (true figure higher - cash netted out would shrink the denominator) with gross debt at only 0.46x EBITDA.
16 consecutive annual increases, including raises through FY2020 when net income fell to $24.0m - the dividend was defended out of FCF, not earnings.
Dividend growth is accelerating, not decaying: g3 12.02% vs g10 5.84%, with +15.3% and +16.9% in the last two years.
risks: 0.62% starting yield: even at 12% compounding it takes roughly 14 years to reach a 3% yield on cost, so the return depends on the multiple holding.
Cyclical end market - FY2020 revenue fell 3.4% and EBITDA more than halved to $110m; a destocking cycle hits earnings and the ~28x P/E simultaneously.
Capital is preferentially returned via buyback ($317.2m in FY2026, about 4.4x the dividend), so the dividend is a residual policy and the low payout may persist by choice.
FY2026 DPS of 1.94 contradicts the filed annual 10-K fact of 1.99 and rests on a quarterly-invariant plus cash reconciliation; if the 10-K note says 1.99, yield and g5 rise slightly (0.63%, 8.89%).
No derivable cash FY2022-FY2026 means net debt/EBITDA and ROIC are bounds, not measurements - a genuine reporting gap in the most recent five years.
EBITDA is built on the Depreciation tag only; if acquired-intangible amortisation is reported separately, EBITDA is understated and historical leverage overstated from FY2018.
flags: FY2026 DPS restated from the filed 1.99 to 1.94 (summed quarterly rates 0.46+0.46+0.51+0.51, reconciled to divPaid/sharesBasic = 1.94232); confirm against the FY2026 10-K dividend note.
netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and roic are null for FY2022-FY2026; rules 7 and 8 were assessed on explicit bounds, not on the defined formula.
Payout fails on the LOW side (15.8% vs the 20% floor) - read as under-distribution, not as distress.
Revenue not derivable FY2009-FY2016; fcfMargin only exists from FY2017.
analysis.sectorNote: AIT is an ordinary industrial distributor (Industrials), not a REIT, insurer or regulated utility, so every rule is applied on its standard basis: FCF = CFO - capex, and dividends/FCF is the payout test. The only sector-flavoured reading is rule 4's direction - for a low-capex distributor throwing off $460m of FCF on $24m of capex, a payout below the 20% floor reflects a buyback-first capital policy rather than reinvestment need, so it is flagged as under-distribution rather than treated as a red flag. Rules 7 and 8 were answered with bounds because the filed cash tag stops at FY2021; both bounds are wide enough that the verdict does not turn on the missing number.

stocks.m: IBP is the #2 national insulation installer with ~250 local branches, and its edge is route density plus national builder master-agreements and manufacturer rebate tiers that a single-market installer cannot replicate on price alone.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (364-365 day durations, 10-K) gives the TOTAL declared per share, which for IBP bundles the regular quarterly dividend with a large annual variable/special dividend declared each February. Regular annual DPS was therefore rebuilt as 4x the regular quarterly rate taken from the instant-dated "rate" facts and the Q2/Q3/Q4 duration facts (which contain no special): FY2021 4x0.30=1.20; FY2022 4x0.315=1.26; FY2023 4x0.33=1.32; FY2024 4x0.35=1.40; FY2025 4x0.37=1.48. The special each year is the residual filed-annual minus regular, which exactly reconciles: 2022 2.16-1.26=0.90 (and the 0.90 fact is filed verbatim at 2022-02-23); 2023 2.22-1.32=0.90; 2024 3.00-1.40=1.60; 2025 3.18-1.48=1.70. Each Q1 duration fact equals regular+special (e.g. 2024-Q1 1.95 = 0.35+1.60; 2025-Q1 2.07 = 0.37+1.70), confirming the decomposition. FY2021 1.20 is all regular (no special that year). No split adjustment applied - see splitAdjustments.

specials.note: IBP declares a large variable/special dividend every February alongside the regular quarterly rate. Specials per share: FY2022 0.90, FY2023 0.90, FY2024 1.60, FY2025 1.70, and FY2026 1.80 (declared Feb 2026, outside the annual window). FY2021 (initiation year) had none. The filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared and the PaymentsOfDividends cash figure BOTH include the special, so headline DPS (3.18 in FY2025) overstates the regular dividend (1.48) by ~2.15x and all payout ratios in fin are total-dividend payouts, not regular-only. Regular-only FY2025 payout would be ~1.48*27.2m shares = ~40m, ~13% of FCF.

issues: Splits: the only split fact is StockholdersEquityNoteStockSplitConversionRatio1 = 19.5 at 2014-02-10, the pre-IPO recapitalisation/stock split done at the February 2014 IPO. No DPS facts exist before 2019, so NO dividend year required split adjustment; splitAdjustments is empty and yearsAdjusted is empty for every year. The FY2013 sharesBasic of 22.03m vs FY2014 30.11m is the IPO share issuance, not an unadjusted basis - FY2012/FY2013 were already restated post-split in the FY2014 10-K, so no share multiplication was applied either.

JUDGEMENT CALL - regular vs total DPS: the filed annual tag mixes the regular quarterly dividend and the February special. I treated the recurring quarterly rate (0.30/0.315/0.33/0.35/0.37) as regular and the February residual as special. Cross-checks that support this: the 0.90 special is filed verbatim as a standalone fact at 2022-02-23; every Q1 duration fact equals regular+special exactly (2022-Q1 1.22~0.315+0.90 with filer rounding, 2023-Q1 1.23=0.33+0.90, 2024-Q1 1.95=0.35+1.60, 2025-Q1 2.07=0.37+1.70, 2026-Q1 2.19=0.39+1.80); and live.regularDividendIfSpecial = 1.48 matches my FY2025 regular exactly. live.ttmDividend 3.34 also reconciles (2.19+0.39+0.39+0.37).

Rounding in filer's own quarterly facts: FY2022 regular was declared at 0.315/qtr but paid/tagged as 0.32 in Q2-Q4 and the YTD facts round (Q3 YTD 1.85 vs 1.22+0.32+0.32=1.86). I used the declared rate 0.315 x4 = 1.26, which reconciles exactly to the filed annual 2.16 (1.26+0.90). Using the rounded 0.32 would give 1.28 and break the reconciliation.

divPaid/sharesBasic cross-check vs TOTAL filed DPS (not regular): FY2021 1.2020 vs 1.20 (+0.2%); FY2022 2.1840 vs 2.16 (+1.1%); FY2023 2.2406 vs 2.22 (+0.9%); FY2024 3.0217 vs 3.00 (+0.7%); FY2025 3.2204 vs 3.18 (+1.3%). All inside 5%. The consistent small positive bias is cash paid on unvested share-based awards (DividendsShareBasedCompensation, 0.8m in FY2025) plus declared-vs-paid timing. No year disagreed materially.

divPaid tag choice: PaymentsOfDividends (cash-flow statement, 7 points from 2019) used over DividendsCommonStockCash (equity statement, 5 points); the two differ by at most 0.4m in any year, immaterial.

g5 and g10 are null: the regular DPS five years before FY2025 is FY2020 = 0 (dividend initiated February 2021), so the CAGR denominator is zero. gMax is the FY2021->FY2025 4-year CAGR of 5.38%/yr. This contradicts priorEstimates.growth5y = 30, which was almost certainly computed off the special-inclusive headline DPS.

Streak = 5 counts FY2021 (0 -> 1.20, initiation) as an increase. If initiation-from-zero is excluded, the streak is 4 (FY2022-FY2025). Each subsequent year is a genuine increase in the regular rate: 1.20 -> 1.26 -> 1.32 -> 1.40 -> 1.48. FY2026 is already running at 0.39/qtr (1.56 annualised), a 6th increase, but its fiscal year is incomplete so it is excluded from dps/fin.

No dividend existed in FY2019 or FY2020, so cut2020 is false rather than null - there was nothing to cut. The FY2019->FY2020 flat zero is recorded as a hold only for completeness; it is a pre-initiation period, not a suspension.

FY2011 appears in the table with StockholdersEquity only (-9.56m); all other fin fields for FY2011 are null. FY2012 has no balance-sheet debt/cash and no revenue tag, so netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and ROIC are null there.

ROIC is null for FY2012 and FY2013 because invested capital (equity + debt - cash) was negative in the pre-IPO leveraged-recap period (FY2013: -71.4m equity + 28.0m debt - 4.1m cash = -47.6m). A negative denominator makes ROIC meaningless rather than large.

Revenue is null for FY2012-FY2015: the RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax family starts 2016 and the legacy SalesRevenueNet series was not included in the table join, so those years are not derivable from this file. FY2016-FY2017 revenue comes from the post-ASC606 tag in the table.

EBITDA uses opIncome + DepreciationAndAmortization (the primary D&A tag, 14 points). The overlapping DepreciationDepletionAndAmortization tag (2020-2025) was not used; only the primary was present in the table join.

Effective tax rate is computed per year from tax/pretax (range 23.6%-38.8%); FY2012 and FY2011 have no usable pretax so the 21% fallback would apply, but ROIC is null there anyway for the reasons above.

FCF is unadjusted cfo - capex and excludes PaymentsToAcquireBusinessesNetOfCashAcquired (51.5m in FY2025), which is how IBP actually deploys most of its cash; payoutFcf therefore understates total capital-allocation intensity for this serial acquirer.

priorEstimates were not used anywhere. For the record they were wrong on growth (30% vs actual 5.4-5.5% regular-DPS CAGR) and on streak (5 matches only if initiation counts); payoutPctFcf 25 is close to the total-dividend FY2025 figure of 29.1%.

normalised.notes: IBP initiated its dividend in February 2021 and has raised the regular quarterly rate every year since (0.30 -> 0.315 -> 0.33 -> 0.35 -> 0.37 -> 0.39 for 2026), a modest ~5.4%/yr compounding. The headline filed DPS is dominated by an annual February variable/special dividend that has grown much faster (0.90 -> 0.90 -> 1.60 -> 1.70 -> 1.80), so any series built on the filed annual tag badly overstates the dividend's reliability - the special is explicitly discretionary and tied to the housing cycle. Total-dividend payout is a comfortable 29% of FCF and 33% of net income in FY2025; regular-only payout is roughly 13% of FCF. Balance sheet is sound at 1.25x net debt/EBITDA with ROIC in the 22-23% range for four straight years, though revenue growth has stalled (2.94bn -> 2.97bn, +1.0% in FY2025) and capex plus buybacks (172.6m in FY2025) now absorb far more cash than the dividend. Cyclical single-family-construction exposure is the main risk to the special.

A consumer reading latest.dps=1.48 next to latest.payoutFcf=0.2912 will wrongly infer the regular dividend absorbs 29% of FCF. The note discloses it, but no machine-readable regular-only field exists.

issues.detail: "summed-quarters" mislabels the actual method for every year. FY2021 1.20 is the filed 364-day annual fact verbatim (and also equals 4x0.30). FY2022-FY2025 were NOT built by summing the four quarterly duration facts - summing them would include the Q1 special (e.g. 2025: 2.07+0.37+0.37+0.37 = 3.18). They were built as 4x the instant-dated rate fact, cross-checked as filed-annual minus special. The label understates the judgement embedded in the number.
issues.suggested: basis "filed" for FY2019/2020/2021; basis "regular-rate-x4" (or "filed-annual-less-special") for FY2022-FY2025.

issues.detail: yearsCovered=5 with fromFy 2021 and toFy 2025 is inconsistent: 2021->2025 spans 4 fiscal years, and gMax=5.3829% is correctly computed as a 4-year CAGR ((1.48/1.20)^(1/4)-1). 5 appears to be a count of data points, not years, and will be read as a 5-year CAGR denominator.
issues.suggested: yearsCovered = 4 (or rename the field to dpsPointsCovered and keep 5 alongside an explicit gMaxYears = 4).

issues.detail: The derivation rules' priority (a) is "filed annual DPS tag with ~1-year duration -> use it", and the rules' own special-detection trigger (filed DPS far ABOVE divPaid/shares) does NOT fire here - filed 3.18 vs divPaid/shares 3.22 agree to 1.3% because the cash paid also includes the variable dividend. The record therefore overrides priority (a) on quarterly-fact evidence rather than on the rule's stated trigger. The override is well evidenced and is what check 7 asks for, but it is a deliberate deviation from the rule hierarchy and should be marked as such, not presented as the default path.
issues.suggested: Keep dps=1.48 regular, but carry the filed annual series alongside it (e.g. dps[].filedTotal = 1.20/2.16/2.22/3.00/3.18) so a downstream consumer can reproduce the rule-(a) series without re-reading the raw file.

issues.detail: The variable dividend has now been declared in five consecutive Februaries (2022 0.90, 2023 0.90, 2024 1.60, 2025 1.70, 2026 1.80) and has grown in three of the four transitions. Calling it "explicitly discretionary" is defensible for a cyclical, but a five-year unbroken run makes a pure regular-only DPS series arguably too conservative for the growth read (regular CAGR 5.4% vs total-DPS CAGR (3.18/1.20)^(1/4)-1 = 27.6%). The true reliability sits between the two.
issues.suggested: State both explicitly: regularCagr4y = 5.38%, totalCagr4y = 27.55%, and note the special has recurred 5/5 years since 2022.

issues.detail: Nulling ROIC for FY2012/FY2013 deviates from the stated rule, which only requires null when equity is missing. Equity is present (FY2013 -71.429m); invested capital is -71.429+27.771+0.255-4.065 = -47.468m (the record says -47.6m, a 0.3% transcription slip). The rule as written would yield 13.078*(1-0.3884)/-47.468 = -0.169.
issues.suggested: Either keep null with the negative-IC rationale (preferred, and already documented) but correct the quoted IC to -47.47m, or return -0.169 per the literal rule. Do not leave the quoted figure at -47.6m.

issues.detail: The streak of 5 counts FY2021 (0 -> 1.20) as an 'increase', i.e. dividend initiation from zero. On a regular-rate basis there have been 4 genuine raises in the data window (1.20 -> 1.26 -> 1.32 -> 1.40 -> 1.48), with a 5th in progress in FY2026 (0.39/qtr, confirmed externally by the ttm 3.34 decomposition). The record self-discloses this in dataQuality.issues, so it is transparent rather than wrong, but a downstream screen reading 'streak: 5' as five consecutive raises will be off by one. Also note the true count only reaches 5 once incomplete FY2026 is included.

issues.detail: External-coherence caveat on the regular-vs-special split. The February variable dividend has now been declared five consecutive years (Feb 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026) and has grown 0.90 -> 0.90 -> 1.60 -> 1.70 -> 1.80, i.e. it behaves like a recurring policy component rather than a one-off. Market-facing data agrees with the record's regular figure (live.regularDividendIfSpecial = 1.48, exact match), so the record is coherent with the vendor, but the headline any external consumer sees is the 3.34 TTM / 3.18 FY2025 figure — 2.26x the record's dps. Yield on the record's series (0.74%) understates the quoted yield (1.67%) by the same factor. Defensible judgement call, fully documented, but it is the single largest divergence between this record and public perception of IBP's dividend.

strengths: ROIC 22-23% for four consecutive years on a 1.25x net-debt/EBITDA balance sheet - high returns without leverage doing the work
FCF 300.8m in FY2025 growing 15.4%/yr over five years, roughly triple the regular dividend's growth rate
Regular quarterly rate raised every single year since initiation (0.30 -> 0.39 for 2026), with total dividends taking only 29% of FCF and 33% of net income
Market cap $5.4B - small enough that acquisitions of local installers still move the numbers
risks: Regular yield of 0.74% is the binding problem: even at 8%/yr growth it would take a decade to reach a useful yield on cost
About 55% of the FY2025 dividend (1.70 of 3.18) is a discretionary February variable payment tied to the housing cycle - a downturn removes it without technically being a cut
Revenue essentially flat in FY2025 (2.94bn -> 2.97bn, +1.0%), so FCF growth is running ahead of the business
Five-year dividend history with no recession test; IBP was private through 2008 and the policy has only existed in a strong housing cycle
Capital allocation favours buybacks and acquisitions (172.6m of repurchases plus 51.5m of deals in FY2025) far ahead of the regular dividend
analysis.assessment: IBP is an excellent business attached to a dividend that is too young and too small to compound for you yet. The operating case is strong - 22.5% ROIC for a fourth straight year, 1.25x net debt/EBITDA, FCF up 15.4%/yr to $300.8m, and total dividends taking a comfortable 29% of that - but the regular dividend of $1.48 against a $199.52 price yields only 0.74%, well under the 1.5% floor, and the committed rate has grown just 5.4%/yr since initiation in 2021. The headline 1.67% yield and ~28%/yr growth both come from the February variable dividend ($1.70 of the $3.18 declared for FY2025), which has now recurred five Februaries running but is explicitly discretionary and tied to single-family construction. The snowball here is a low-yield, low-committed-growth one where more than half the cash depends on the housing cycle staying good, and the payout only reaches a healthy 29% of FCF because of that discretionary half - regular-only it is 13%. The most likely thing to break it is a housing downturn: the special disappears, the quoted yield halves overnight without a formal cut, and flat FY2025 revenue (+1.0%) suggests the cycle is already rolling over.

normalised.notes:
FISCAL LABELS — the reviewer's block, addressed head-on. Exponent runs a 52/53-week fiscal year ending on the Friday/Saturday closest to Dec 31, so period ends alternate between late December and the first days of January. Applying the stated rule literally (label = calendar year of the period end) produces THREE DUPLICATE labels — 2010-01-01 and 2010-12-31 both map to 2010, 2016-01-01 and 2016-12-30 both to 2016, 2021-01-01 and 2021-12-31 both to 2021 — and three gaps (2013, 2019, 2024). Duplicate keys are not cosmetic here: under the literal rule "FY2016" would carry two different DPS values (0.60 and 0.36), the streak and every label-keyed CAGR become undefined, and dps would no longer be a function of fy. The reviewer offered two remedies; I have taken the second verbatim. The primary fy field keeps the issuer's own convention (an end date of Jan 1-3 belongs to the prior calendar year), which is unique, consecutive and is what Exponent itself calls these years; and EVERY dps row, fin row and the latest block now also carries an explicit fyLiteral field holding the rule-conformant label. Under the literal rule latest.fy is 2026 (the 10-K for the year ended 2026-01-02), stated here explicitly so no consumer is surprised. The period end remains the unambiguous primary key on every row.

EIGHT rows (not four, as the original record wrongly claimed) differ between the two labellings: ends 2009-01-02, 2010-01-01, 2014-01-03, 2016-01-01, 2020-01-03, 2021-01-01, 2025-01-03 and 2026-01-02, labelled 2008, 2009, 2013, 2015, 2019, 2020, 2024 and 2025 respectively, versus literal 2009, 2010, 2014, 2016, 2020, 2021, 2025 and 2026. The other ten rows are identical under both rules.

WHERE THE REVIEWERS ARE WRONG. (1) The adversarial reviewer says the filed tag IncomeLossFromContinuingOperationsBeforeIncomeTaxesExtraordinaryItemsNoncontrollingInterest "was simply not pulled into the table" and should be pulled. It cannot be: families.pretax carries only "primary" and "candidates" — it has NO "series" block (only dps, divPaid, cfo and capex do), so that tag's VALUES do not exist anywhere in this source file. Its 9 points are a header count, not data. Deriving pretax is the only option available, not a choice. (2) The same reviewer says the presence of a ProfitLoss candidate signals a non-controlling interest and biases pretax = NetIncomeLoss + tax. The raw table refutes this: in all TEN years carrying a filed pretax value, NetIncomeLoss + IncomeTaxExpenseBenefit reproduces it to the dollar — including FY2017 (41,305 + 41,204 = 82,509) and FY2018 (72,254 + 21,063 = 93,317), the two years where BOTH the filed pre-NCI pretax tag and the ProfitLoss candidate are present. If NCI were non-zero in those years the identity would fail; it does not, so NCI is zero and ProfitLoss duplicates NetIncomeLoss. The derived FY2019-FY2025 rates are therefore filed-quality and the ROIC values stand unchanged. (3) The split handling was challenged only by implication and survives re-derivation: it is confirmed, not merely asserted, by the fact that FY2016's filed annual DPS of 0.36 is NOT 4x its own as-filed quarterly rate of 0.18.

Dividend picture: initiated in fiscal 2013, 13 straight annual increases through FY2025 on a today's-basis series of 0.15 -> 1.20, with no cut or hold anywhere including 2020-2021. Growth is decelerating cleanly (10y 14.9%, 5y 9.6%, 3y 7.7%) and the declared quarterly rate has already gone to 0.31 for the year ending Jan 2027 (0.62 declared through H1, an annualised 1.24, matching live ttmDividend 1.23). Coverage is comfortable: latest payout 50.3% of FCF and 58.1% of net income, with a net CASH position of 221.9M (net debt/EBITDA -1.71x) and no borrowings at all in the filings. Buybacks are the swing user of cash (97.1M in the latest year, 155.9M in FY2022), not the dividend.

issues.detail: The record knowingly departs from the stated labelling rule ('fiscal-year label = calendar year of the period END date'). fiscalYearEnd is '--01-03', i.e. a January FYE, and by the rule's own worked example ('a March FYE means FY2026 ended 2026-03-31') the period ended 2026-01-02 must be labelled FY2026, not FY2025. The deviation is not limited to the four rows the record admits to: EIGHT of the eighteen rows are shifted by one year versus the literal rule - ends 2009-01-02 (labelled 2008), 2010-01-01 (2009), 2014-01-03 (2013), 2016-01-01 (2015), 2020-01-03 (2019), 2021-01-01 (2020), 2025-01-03 (2024), 2026-01-02 (2025). Any downstream consumer joining this record to price, rating or calendar data by fiscal-year key will be off by one on those rows, and 'latest.fy 2025' will silently disagree with a live feed that calls the 10-K ended 2026-01-02 fiscal 2026. The collision argument the record raises is real (2010-01-01/2010-12-31, 2016-01-01/2016-12-30, 2021-01-01/2021-12-31 all collide under the literal rule), but the fix is to disambiguate explicitly, not to silently re-base the whole series.
issues.suggested: Either (a) apply the literal rule and disambiguate the three collisions (e.g. 2010a/2010b or keep the period end as the primary key), giving latest.fy = '2026' (end 2026-01-02), FY2025 = end 2025-01-03, FY2020 = end 2020-01-03, FY2016 = end 2016-01-01, FY2014 = end 2014-01-03, FY2010 = end 2010-01-01, FY2009 = end 2009-01-02; or (b) keep the company-convention labels but add an explicit second field (e.g. fyLiteral) carrying the rule-conformant label on every row, and state that latest.fy under the literal rule is 2026.

The record asserts 'PRETAX MISSING from FY2019 onward' and derives pretax = netIncome + IncomeTaxExpenseBenefit. Two problems. (i) A filed pretax tag DOES exist for exactly those years: families.pretax.candidates includes IncomeLossFromContinuingOperationsBeforeIncomeTaxesExtraordinaryItemsNoncontrollingInterest with 9 points running 2017-12-29 to 2026-01-02 - it was simply not the primary and never pulled into the table, so the claim that no filed figure exists is unverified rather than true. (ii) The identity used is pretax = NetIncomeLoss + tax, but a ProfitLoss candidate (9 points, 2017-12-29 to 2026-01-02) exists alongside NetIncomeLoss, which is the signature of a non-controlling interest; where NCI is non-zero the correct identity is ProfitLoss + tax, and the derived effective rate (28.03% in FY2025) is biased. Separately, the literal derivation rule offers a 21% fallback when pretax is unavailable, which would give FY2025 NOPAT 94,632k and ROIC 0.5619 rather than 0.5119 - a 5.0pp spread on the headline ROIC depending on which reading is taken. Not blocked because the record's method is the more defensible of the two and is internally exact, but the sourcing claim is wrong and the number is method-dependent.
issues.suggested: Pull IncomeLossFromContinuingOperationsBeforeIncomeTaxesExtraordinaryItemsNoncontrollingInterest for FY2017-FY2025 and use the filed pretax; if deriving, use ProfitLoss + tax and confirm ProfitLoss == NetIncomeLoss. Restate the issue text to 'primary pretax tag ends at FY2018; secondary filed tag IncomeLossFromContinuingOperationsBeforeIncomeTaxesExtraordinaryItemsNoncontrollingInterest covers FY2017-FY2025 and was/was not used', and disclose that the 21%-fallback reading would put FY2025 ROIC at 0.5619.

analysis.assessment: Exponent is a $3.3B net-cash consultancy yielding 1.76% on a $1.20 regular dividend ($1.81% on the new $0.31 quarterly rate) with 13 straight increases and a 9.6% five-year dividend CAGR — 9 of the 10 rules pass, including payout at 50.3% of FY2025 free cash flow and ROIC of 51%. The snowball here is quality over speed: a low starting yield compounded by high-single-digit raises off a balance sheet with $222M of net cash and zero borrowings, with buybacks ($97M in FY2025) rather than the dividend as the swing use of cash. The one failure is the one that matters most over a decade — free cash flow compounded at just 4.5% over five years (net income 5.1%) against a dividend growing 9.6%, which is exactly why the FCF payout has drifted from 40.5% in FY2020 to 50.3% now and why dividend growth has already decelerated from 14.9% (10y) to 7.7% (3y). Revenue growth of roughly 4% a year on a headcount-bound fee-for-service model is the structural constraint: Exponent cannot scale billings faster than it can hire credentialled experts. The thing most likely to break it is not the balance sheet but arithmetic — if FCF keeps compounding at ~4-5%, the raises must converge down to that rate within a few years or the payout runs past 60%, so underwrite this as a 5-7% dividend grower, not a 10% one.
analysis.moat: Failure-analysis and expert-witness consulting where court-tested, Daubert-surviving credentials are the product — clients facing litigation or a recall cannot substitute a cheaper unproven expert.
strengths: Zero debt and $221.9M net cash (net debt/EBITDA -1.71x); no leverage competing with the dividend.
ROIC 51.2% on an asset-light model; 21% FCF margin on $582M of revenue.
13 consecutive increases including raises straight through 2020 and 2021, with the FY2026 quarterly rate already lifted to $0.31.
Payout 50.3% of FCF leaves real runway, and buybacks ($97.1M in FY2025, $155.9M in FY2022) are the flexible cash user, not the dividend.
risks: 5-yr FCF CAGR 4.47% trails the 9.57% dividend CAGR — the payout ratio has risen from 40.5% (FY2020) to 50.3% (FY2025) and cannot absorb that gap for another five years.
Dividend growth is already converging down: 14.9% (10y) -> 9.6% (5y) -> 7.7% (3y) -> ~3.3% on the latest declared raise. The forward rate is likely mid-single-digit, below the rule-3 threshold.

Headcount-bound revenue model (~1,012 employees, ~4% revenue growth) — growth requires hiring scarce credentialled experts; utilisation and billing-rate cycles drive earnings volatility (FY2022 FCF fell to 81.8M).
1.76% starting yield means total return depends on multiple retention at a premium valuation; a de-rating is not cushioned by income.
Key-person and reputational concentration: a single high-profile testimony failure damages the exact asset the moat rests on.
analysis.sectorNote: No sector adjustment needed — Exponent is an ordinary asset-light operating company, so FCF = CFO - capex is the right payout base and rule 8 is read as an outright net-cash pass (the negative -1.71x is not leverage). The only read-through worth flagging is rule 7: with essentially no debt and a small capital base, ROIC of 51% reflects business model, not incremental returns on reinvested capital, since Exponent returns most cash rather than reinvesting it.

A special dividend shows the opposite signature - filed DPS far ABOVE cash paid per share in one year - and no year shows that. FY2024's rise to $3.30 is a step-up, not a special: the tagged quarterly rate moved from $0.75 (Q1, Q2) to $0.90 (Q3), and the implied Q4 of $0.90 (3.30 - 2.40 YTD-Q3) is the same rate, so the raise landed in Q3 2024 and carried forward. issues: CONFIDENCE IS SPLIT. Dividend series: HIGH confidence - filed annual tag on every one of 16 years, no splits, divPaid/sharesBasic agrees within 0.13%-4.16% in all 16 years, no specials, streak and CAGRs all recompute exactly. Balance-sheet and profitability fields: LOW confidence - netDebt/netDebtToEbitda null for 14 of 17 years including the latest, capex null for 13 of 17 years, ROIC computed with debt forced to zero in the denominator, EBITDA nulled for the last two years, and FY2025 net income not derivable on the filed basis. The object-level flag is therefore 'medium', not 'high'.

BLOCK FIXED - FY2025 NET INCOME SET TO NULL. The reviewer is right. The extract's NetIncomeLoss family runs 2009-2024 with a 2013 gap and has NO point for 2025-12-31. The previous record substituted pretax minus tax ($974,564,000 - $223,330,000 = $751,234,000) and presented it beside FY2022-FY2024 payoutNi figures computed on the FILED tag. Those two bases are demonstrably not the same series in this dataset. Recomputing pretax-tax against filed NetIncomeLoss for every year with both: FY2011 0.00%, FY2012 -0.29%, FY2014 -0.87%, FY2015 0.00%, FY2016 0.00%, FY2017 0.00%, FY2018 0.00%, FY2019 0.00%, FY2020 0.00%, FY2021 -0.29%, then FY2022 +17.51% ($554,714k derived vs $472,068k filed), FY2023 +2.53% ($591,182k vs $576,601k), FY2024 +53.05% ($720,129k vs $470,518k - a $249.6m gap). Because FY2024 uses the filed tag and FY2025 would have used the derived one, the previously reported fall in payoutNi from 23.98% to 18.11% was an artefact of switching bases, not a real move. fin[2025].netIncome, fin[2025].payoutNi and latest.payoutNi are therefore null. The filed figure IS retrievable - families.netIncome.candidates lists NetIncomeLossAvailableToCommonStockholdersBasic (15 points, 2010-2025) and ProfitLoss (15 points, 2011-2025), both of which cover 2025-12-31 - but neither series was pulled into this extract, so it must be fetched rather than substituted.

FY2024 AND FY2022 FILED NET INCOME ARE THEMSELVES SUSPECT (kept, but do not compare payoutNi across years). The FY2024 NetIncomeLoss point of $470,518,000 implies an effective tax rate of 1 - 470,518/939,247 = 49.9%, against the filed IncomeTaxExpenseBenefit/pretax of 219,118/939,247 = 23.3%. It also falls 18.4% from FY2023's $576,601,000 while revenue rose 12.4% ($3,089m vs $2,749m), pretax rose 21.7% ($939.2m vs $771.7m) and tax rose 21.4%. FY2022 shows the same pattern (implied ETR 34.3% vs filed 22.8%). Both are most likely mis-scoped contexts (segment, parent-only Schedule II, or a restated fact) rather than the consolidated attributable figure. They are the filed primary tag so they are retained under the never-invent rule, but payoutNi for FY2022 and FY2024 is NOT comparable with FY2011-FY2021. On a consistent pretax-minus-tax basis the same years would read: FY2022 0.1510, FY2023 0.1585, FY2024 0.1567.

FY2013 NET INCOME IS DERIVED AND IS KEPT (unlike FY2025). fin[2013].netIncome = $158,701,000 = pretax $245,006,000 minus tax $86,305,000, because NetIncomeLoss has no 2013-12-31 point. Unlike FY2025 the derivation is locally validated: the immediately adjacent years reconcile tightly on the same basis (FY2012 -0.29%, FY2014 -0.87%), and the whole FY2011-FY2021 block reconciles within 0.9%. FY2025's adjacent year (FY2024) diverges by 53%, so the basis is not validated there. payoutNi for FY2013 (0.1579) rests on this derived denominator.

EBITDA NULLED FOR FY2024 AND FY2025 (convention break, reviewer accepted remedy). EBITDA is opIncome + D&A with opIncome taken as pretax + InterestExpense, since no operating-income tag exists. The InterestExpense family stops at 2023-12-31 and the table carries no interest value for FY2024 or FY2025, so opIncome is not derivable for those years. The previous record reported $957,447,000 and $993,864,000 on a pretax + D&A basis, understating them by roughly the $26.6-30.6m interest run-rate (about 2.7-3.1% of EBITDA) versus every earlier year - above the comparability threshold, and the schema has no per-row basis marker to make the break machine-visible. The alternative tag InterestPaidNet (10 points, 2016-2025) would close the gap but its series is not included in this extract, so it cannot be pulled. Both years are therefore null. Nothing is lost downstream: netDebtToEbitda is null for those years anyway for want of a debt tag.

ROIC IS RETAINED FOR FY2024-FY2025 DESPITE THE SAME MISSING INTEREST, and here is the justification. ROIC = opIncome x (1 - tax/pretax) / (equity + debt - cash). For FY2024-FY2025 opIncome falls back to pretax alone, which UNDERSTATES the numerator by about 2.8%; meanwhile the debt-free denominator OVERSTATES ROIC by roughly 25-30% relative. The denominator error dominates and is disclosed below, so the figure is directionally caveated either way, whereas nulling would remove the latest-year ROIC entirely. EBITDA by contrast is a level series whose only consumer is already null, so a silent break there is pure cost. Recomputed and confirmed: FY2024 939,247 x (1 - 0.23329) / (2,259,041 - 687,821) = 0.4583; FY2025 974,564 x (1 - 0.22916) / (2,445,902 - 756,227) = 0.4446.

NET DEBT: not derivable for 14 of 17 years including the latest. The debtLT family (LongTermDebt) has only 2 points (FY2011 $300.0m, FY2012 $374.4m) and there is no debtCur family at all, so netDebt and netDebtToEbitda are null for FY2009-FY2010 and FY2013-FY2025. Computed only for FY2011 ($300,000k - $136,078k = $163,922k, 0.5872x EBITDA) and FY2012 ($374,433k - $112,214k = $262,219k, 0.8588x). Primerica demonstrably carries senior notes throughout (interest expense of $26.6-35.0m runs every year from 2011 to 2023 in the table), but no debt tag was captured, so the balance is not in the data. The external reviewer's suggestion to insert an externally-known ~$600m senior-note balance is declined: that would be inventing a number the extract does not contain. The honest statement is that leverage cannot be measured from this record, only that non-zero debt exists and the interest run-rate is small relative to $900m+ of CFO.

ROIC IS COMPUTED WITH DEBT = ZERO in the invested-capital denominator for every year except FY2011 and FY2012, because the debt tags are missing. That overstates ROIC for FY2013-FY2025 by roughly the ratio of debt to equity. ROIC is null for FY2009 and FY2010 (no pretax point - the pretax family starts 2011) and for FY2013 (no StockholdersEquity point). Effective tax = tax/pretax was available every year from 2011 on, so the 21% fallback was never needed.

ROIC FY2021 (0.9356) is an outlier artefact, not a real result: StockholdersEquity collapsed to $925,427,000 at 2021-12-31 (from $1,835,885,000 in 2020, back to $2,031,254,000 in 2022) on AOCI swings, which shrinks the denominator. Not comparable.

CAPEX AND THE MIXED FCF BASIS. The PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment family has only 3 points (FY2009 $4,894k, FY2010 $9,864k, FY2011 $3,913k). For FY2012 the table carries no capex key, so PaymentsToAcquireAssetsInvestingActivities ($6,594,000, the tagHints last value at 2012-12-31, same order of magnitude as the PP&E figures) was substituted and is named in capexTag. For FY2013-FY2025 no capex-like tag exists at all - the remaining Payments* tags are securities purchases, claims payments, buybacks, dividends, tax withholding and lease payments - so capex is null and FCF equals CFO for those 13 years. The FCF series therefore sits on three definitions across 17 years. This IS machine-visible: capexTag names the tag where capex was measured and is null exactly where FCF = CFO. Consequence: payoutFcf for FY2013-FY2025 and latest.fcfMargin are CFO-based (a floor on the true FCF payout), and growth.fcfGrowth5 compares two CFO-only endpoints so it is internally consistent but is a CFO CAGR, not an FCF CAGR.
