rules.note: Current declared quarterly rate is $1.20 (2026 Q1 and Q2 both tagged), so the regular annual DPS on the current basis is $4.80 = 1.64%. TTM $4.64 = 1.59%. The stale FY2025 filed total of $4.16 = 1.43% would fail; every current-basis measure passes, but only just - this is a bottom-of-band yield and the whole case rests on growth.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: STRONG. g3 23.66%, g10 20.58%, and the 2026 raise to $1.20/qtr is another +15.4% on an annualised basis. No split adjustment needed (no split since the April 2010 IPO). gMax of 42.74% is an artefact of the $0.02 initiation base and is not used.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: FAILS THE FLOOR, NOT THE CEILING - this is under-distribution, not strain. Insurer, so FCF = CFO - capex is the right basis, but no capex tag exists FY2013-FY2025 so the denominator is unreduced CFO; where capex was disclosed it ran 1.4-5.3% of CFO, so a true FCF payout is roughly 15-16%, still below 20%. On net income it is the same story: ~15.7-16.3% on a consistent pretax-minus-tax basis (FY2023 15.85%, FY2024 15.67%). Primerica returns far more through buybacks - $450.0m in FY2025 - so dividends plus repurchases are 65.0% of CFO.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to still be fast
rules.note: Not window-limited: FY2009 is present in the data with zero dividends paid and the IPO was April 2010, so the streak provably cannot extend earlier. Prior research says 16, which counts FY2010's $0.02 initiation over a zero base; the conservative 15 is used. Either figure sits mid-band.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: THE CENTRAL TENSION. CFO grew from $643.4m (FY2020) to $901.2m (FY2025), 6.97%/yr, while the dividend grew three times faster. Net income is not a usable cross-check here - the filed NetIncomeLoss tag is internally inconsistent in FY2022 and FY2024 (implied effective tax rates of 34.3% and 49.9% against filed 22.8% and 23.3%) and has no FY2025 point. Revenue grew 8.2%/yr FY2020-FY2025 ($2,217.5m to $3,291.7m), so ~7-8% is the honest underlying rate. The gap has been funded by payout-ratio expansion off a very low base plus a 19% reduction in share count over the same five years.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: STRONG even after heavy haircutting. Computed as pretax x (1 - 22.9%) / (equity $2,445.9m - cash $756.2m) with debt forced to zero because no debt tag exists after FY2012; the record's own estimate is that this overstates ROIC by 25-30% relative, which still leaves ~32-35%. FY2021's 93.6% is an AOCI-driven equity-collapse artefact and is ignored. The trend FY2016-FY2025 (23.6% -> 44.5%) is genuine and reflects a capital-light agent-distribution model.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.value: null (insurer; also not derivable after FY2012)
rules.note: Two reasons for null. (a) Primerica is a life insurer - net debt/EBITDA is not a meaningful solvency measure for a business whose liabilities are policy reserves; RBC ratio is the right metric and is not in this data. (b) Mechanically, the LongTermDebt family stops at FY2012, so leverage cannot be measured from the extract at all. What can be said: where it was measurable it was low (0.59x in FY2011, 0.86x in FY2012), interest expense ran only $26.6-35.0m/yr against $900m+ of CFO through FY2023, and cash was $756.2m at FY2025. No evidence of balance-sheet stress; no measured figure either.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.value: 130,000-rep licensed sales force selling term life to middle-income households
rules.note: The moat is distribution, not product. Term life is a commodity; reaching a household earning $50-100k that will not seek out insurance is not. Primerica recruits its reps from the same demographic it sells to, licenses them, and pays them as independent contractors - a network built over 50 years that no direct-to-consumer insurer has replicated, because the customer acquisition cost of reaching this segment through advertising exceeds the policy economics. The investment-products cross-sell rides the same force for free.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/2021; a cut anywhere in the window fails
rules.value: No cut or hold in 16 years of data
rules.note: DPS rose straight through the pandemic: $1.36 (2019) -> $1.60 (2020) -> $1.88 (2021). Zero flat years and zero cuts in the entire FY2010-FY2025 series. 2008 is outside the window and untestable - Primerica did not exist as a public company until the April 2010 IPO, so there is no financial-crisis behaviour to judge.

analysis.assessment: Primerica is a high-quality compounder whose dividend is simply too small yet: $4.80 annualised on a $291.91 share is a 1.64% starting yield, grown at 21.06%/yr over five years, and costing only 15.1% of $901.2m of operating cash flow. The payout runway is enormous - the ratio could triple and still sit inside a comfortable band - and ROIC of 44.5% (perhaps 33% after adjusting for the debt-free denominator the data forces) on a capital-light distribution model means the growth is self-funded. The thing most likely to break it is arithmetic, not credit: cash flow is compounding at 6.97%/yr against a dividend compounding at 21.06%, so the last decade of raises has been payout-ratio expansion plus a 55% reduction in share count since 2010, and once the ratio reaches a normal 30-40% the dividend must decelerate toward the high single digits unless Primerica finds growth. The real risk is the sales force - 130,000 reps is the entire moat, and recruitment stalling would hit new-policy issuance, investment-product flows and the buyback that levers per-share results all at once. Leverage is unmeasurable from this data (no debt tag after FY2012) and net income for FY2025 is not retrievable on the filed basis, so the safety case rests on cash flow, which is unambiguous.
analysis.moat: Primerica reaches middle-income households that no direct-to-consumer insurer can profitably advertise to, through 130,000 licensed part-time reps recruited from that same demographic over fifty years - a distribution network, not a product, and one that cannot be bought or rebuilt at the price of a term-life premium.

For rule 4 the insurer convention FCF = CFO - capex is used as instructed, but capex is untagged FY2013-FY2025 so the denominator is unreduced CFO; disclosed capex historically ran 1.4-5.3% of CFO, so the true FCF payout is roughly 15-16% rather than 15.1% and the rule-4 conclusion is unchanged. stocks.m: Category-leading listed real-assets specialist - a multi-decade REIT, infrastructure and preferred-securities track record that consultants screen on and that sticky closed-end-fund and institutional mandates are priced off, not a business won on fee level.

normalised.dpsMethod: REGULAR annual DPS = sum of the four quarterly CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared rate facts inside each calendar fiscal year (FYE 12-31). The filed ANNUAL (FY, ~364-day) CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared fact is NOT the regular dividend for CNS: it bundles the year-end special. Quarterly declared rates exist 2013-2026 and are perfectly level within each year (4 x Q rate = 0.80/0.88/1.00/1.04/1.12/1.32/1.44/1.56/1.80/2.20/2.28/2.36/2.48 for FY2013-FY2025), so special = filed annual minus 4 x quarterly rate. FY2012 has no declared-quarterly facts, but CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid shows Q3-2012 = 0.18 and 9M-2012 = 0.54 (= 3 x 0.18), fixing the FY2012 regular rate at 0.18/qtr -> 0.72 regular, 1.50 special. FY2009 has no DPS tag at all; divPaid / weighted basic shares = 0.2001 (= 4 x 0.05) with no evidence of a special, so FY2009 regular = 0.20 (basis derived-from-cash). FY2010 (divPaid/share 2.3973) and FY2011 (filed 1.60, divPaid/share 1.6003) clearly contain large specials that cannot be separated from the regular rate with any fact in this file, so no regular DPS is reported for those two years. Cross-check divPaid/sharesBasic vs filed annual DPS matches within 0.2% for EVERY year 2009-2025, confirming declared = paid in the same fiscal year and confirming the share basis. No split adjustment applied (splitFacts empty; weighted basic shares rise smoothly 42.3M -> 51.2M).

dps.basis: summed-quarters (4 x 0.18 CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid rate; no declared-quarterly facts)

specials.note: CNS paid a year-end special dividend every year from at least 2010 through 2021, then stopped. Specials separated per year (filed annual DPS minus 4 x quarterly declared rate): FY2012 1.50, FY2013 1.00, FY2014 1.00, FY2015 0.50, FY2016 0.50, FY2017 1.00, FY2018 2.50, FY2019 2.00, FY2020 1.00, FY2021 1.25. FY2010 (total 2.3973/sh) and FY2011 (total 1.60/sh) also contain specials but the regular/special split is not derivable from the facts in this file. FY2022-FY2025: none - filed annual DPS equals 4 x the quarterly rate exactly. This is why the FILED annual DPS series falls in 2013, 2015, 2019, 2020 and 2022 while the REGULAR dividend rose in every one of those years; treating the filed series as the dividend would produce five phantom cuts. live.ttmDividend 2.63 is roughly (not exactly) consistent with 2 x 0.62 + 2 x 0.67 = 2.58, i.e. purely regular; regularDividendIfSpecial is null because no special has been paid since 2021.

issues: SPECIALS, not splits, are the whole story here. splitFacts is empty and weighted basic shares rise smoothly from 42.339M (2009) to 51.168M (2025) with no step, so NO split adjustment was made to any year and splitAdjustments is empty. The one share-count step in the file is CommonStockSharesOutstanding jumping 46.31M (2017) -> 52.58M (2019) -> 55.05M (2022) -> 49.16M (2023); that is a tagging/definition change (issued incl. unvested restricted shares vs outstanding), not a split - weighted basic shares over the same span go 46.79M -> 47.27M -> 48.78M -> 49.31M with no discontinuity, and the 2026-07-23 cover count of 51.42M agrees with FY2025 basic. Nothing was divided or multiplied.

The filed annual DPS tag (CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared, FY duration) includes the year-end special in every year 2010-2021. Using it as-is would show cuts in FY2013 (2.22->1.80), FY2015 (1.88->1.50), FY2019 (3.82->3.44), FY2020 (3.44->2.56) and FY2022 (3.05->2.20). All five are specials rolling off; the regular quarterly rate rose in each of those years. dps[].val is the REGULAR series only.

Cross-check divPaid/sharesBasic vs filed annual DPS agrees within 0.2% in EVERY year 2009-2025 (2013: 1.8001 vs 1.80; 2018: 3.8227 vs 3.82; 2021: 3.0540 vs 3.05; 2025: 2.4805 vs 2.48). No year disagreed. This also confirms declared and paid fall in the same fiscal year, so the special-vs-regular split is not a timing artifact.
FY2010 regular DPS NOT derivable: no DPS tag before 2011 and no quarterly facts; total paid 2.3973/sh obviously contains a large special. Omitted from dps rather than guessed.

FY2011 regular DPS NOT derivable: filed annual 1.60 (confirmed by divPaid/shares 1.6003) but no quarterly rate facts for 2011 or earlier, so the regular/special split is unknowable from this file. Omitted from dps. This is the only reason the streak window starts at FY2012.

FY2012 regular rate (0.18/qtr -> 0.72) is inferred from CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid, not from declared-quarterly facts: Q3-2012 = 0.18 and 9M-2012 = 0.54. Judgement call; it is consistent with the 0.20/qtr declared rate that first appears in Q1-2013. If wrong, gMax and the streak endpoint move.

FY2009 regular DPS 0.20 is derived from cash (8.472M / 42.339M basic = 0.2001 = 4 x 0.05) with no filed DPS fact to confirm it and no way to rule out a special. It is an isolated point (2010 and 2011 blank), so it was deliberately NOT used as a CAGR endpoint - a 2009->2025 CAGR of ~17%/yr off a post-crisis trough would be misleading. gMax uses the contiguous regular series 2012->2025 (13 years, 9.98%/yr).

Streak: 13 consecutive increases in the regular dividend, FY2013 through FY2025, running back to the first year of the reliable regular series, so windowLimited = true and the true streak is very likely longer (priorEstimates guessed 19; these filings can neither confirm nor refute the pre-2012 years). No cut or hold in the regular rate anywhere in the window, including FY2020/FY2021 (1.44 -> 1.56 -> 1.80), so cut2020 = false and cutsOrHolds is empty. The FY2021 special of 1.25 was the last special paid.

REVENUE is null for FY2021-FY2025. The Revenues tag in the join stops at 2020 and the per-year table carries no revenue for 2021+, even though the families block lists RevenueFromContractWithCustomerIncludingAssessedTax covering 2016-2025; that series is not in the table, so it could not be used without inventing numbers. Consequence: latest.fcfMargin is null.

FY2025 CFO is NEGATIVE (-120.444M) against net income of +153.2M, so FY2025 FCF = -126.423M. This is almost certainly consolidated-fund / seed-investment purchases running through operating activities (see PaymentsToAcquireMarketableSecurities 383.4M and ProceedsFromPaymentsToMinorityShareholders 228.7M in tagHints), not an operating collapse. Consequences: latest.payoutFcf is null and fcfGrowth5 is null because the 2025 endpoint is <= 0. FCF-based payout is unusable for CNS without unconsolidating the funds; payoutNi 0.828 is the meaningful latest payout. priorEstimates' 60% FCF payout is not reproducible in any year here.

NO DEBT TAG EXISTS in the file (no debtLT / debtCur family, nothing debt-like in tagHints). Debt was therefore treated as zero, so netDebt = -cash in every year and netDebtToEbitda is negative throughout (-0.41 to -2.38). Directionally right for an unlevered asset manager, but it is an assumption, not a filed fact.

Effective tax rate is tax/pretax only for FY2009-FY2020. The table has no pretax for FY2021-FY2025 (the pretax family switches tags in 2019 and the join kept the older one), so the 21% fallback was used for ROIC in those five years. Sanity check: NI+tax implies ~20.9% for 2021 and ~23.6% for 2024, so the fallback is close but FY2023-FY2025 ROIC is slightly overstated.

FY2009 effective tax computes to 108% (tax 4.490M on pretax 4.154M, net loss -1.710M). FY2009 EBITDA and ROIC are null anyway (no D&A tagged for 2009, no equity for 2009) and payoutNi is null because net income is negative.

ROIC is mechanically unstable for this filer because the denominator (equity + debt - cash) is small and cash-dominated: it exceeds 100% in 2016, 2017 and 2019, and hits 290% in FY2021 (equity 255.2M less cash 184.4M leaves invested capital of only 70.8M) and 189% in FY2022. Artifacts of the prescribed formula on a cash-rich, asset-light balance sheet, not real returns. FY2023-FY2025 (0.67 / 0.42 / 0.34) look lower mainly because equity ballooned to 562M.

Payout ratios above 1.0 in many years (payoutNi > 1 in 2010-2015 and 2017-2020; payoutFcf 5.72 in 2012) are real: specials were paid out of accumulated cash and exceeded both earnings and FCF in those years. On the regular dividend alone the payout was far lower.

FY2023 capex of 56.986M is 5-14x every other year (2.4M-11.7M) - consistent with a one-off office/leasehold build-out. It is the filer's own PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment tag and was left unadjusted, but it depresses FY2023 FCF and inflates that year's payoutFcf.

normalised.notes: Cohen & Steers, FYE 12-31, no splits. The only real normalisation problem is that the filed annual DPS tag bundles a year-end special in every year from 2010 through 2021 (largest 2.50 in FY2018 and 2.00 in FY2019). Specials stopped after FY2021 and the regular dividend has kept rising (0.67/qtr declared in 2026). The balance sheet is net cash in every year with no tagged debt. FY2025 operating cash flow is negative because consolidated-fund investment activity runs through CFO, which makes FCF-based payout meaningless for the latest year - use the 82.8% net-income payout instead.

issues.detail: Rule (a) says to use the filed ~1-year annual DPS tag when present; the record deliberately overrides it with summed quarterly rates for every year 2012-2021. I verified the override is correct on the merits (filed annual exceeds 4x the level quarterly rate by a clean round amount in exactly those years, and only those years), but it is a documented departure from the stated priority order and a downstream consumer expecting rule (a) will see a different series than the filer's headline number. The departure is disclosed in dataQuality, so this is not a block.
issues.suggested: Keep the regular series as-is, but also carry the filed annual value per year (e.g. filedAnnual: 3.82 alongside val: 1.32 for FY2018) so consumers can reconcile to the 10-K without recomputing.

issues.detail: dpsAllFacts contains only Q1, Q2 and Q3 declared rate facts for every year - there is no Q4 fact anywhere in the file. The claim that the four quarterly rates are 'perfectly level within each year' is directly demonstrated only for Q1-Q3 (the 9M YTD facts equal 3x the rate). For FY2022-FY2025 the identity filed annual = 4x rate independently proves Q4 = Q1-Q3. For FY2013-FY2021 the Q4 regular rate is an ASSUMPTION, because the annual is contaminated by the special, so any Q4 rate change in those years would be silently absorbed into the computed special. The assumption is well supported by the observed pattern of raising at Q1 (Q1-2026 0.67 vs Q4-2025 0.62) but it is not a filed fact for 2013-2021.
issues.suggested: Add an explicit dataQuality line: 'Q4 declared rate is not filed in any year; regular DPS for FY2013-FY2021 assumes Q4 equals the Q1-Q3 rate, validated by the exact 4x identity in FY2022-FY2025 and by the rate always stepping up at Q1.'

issues.detail: FY2009 (0.20, derived-from-cash) sits in the dps array separated from the next entry (FY2012) by a two-year hole, because FY2010 and FY2011 were omitted as non-derivable. Any consumer that naively computes a CAGR or a max-span growth rate off the array's first and last elements gets 2.48/0.20 over 16 years = 17.1%/yr, which the record itself says is misleading. The record's own growth block correctly starts at FY2012, so nothing in this record is wrong, but the array shape invites the error. FY2009's own value is confirmed (8472/42339 = 0.20010 = 4 x 0.05).
issues.suggested: Either drop the FY2009 entry from dps[] and record it only in notes, or add a flag such as contiguous:false / excludeFromGrowth:true on it.

The same standard applied to FY2009 would admit FY2011 at 1.60 with a special-unknown flag. No computed metric changes either way (growth and streak both start at FY2012), so this is presentational.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.value: 82.8% of net income (FCF payout not computable)
rules.note: Asset manager, so FCF = CFO - capex is the intended basis, but FY2025 CFO is -120.4M because consolidated-fund/seed investment purchases run through operating activities, giving FCF -126.4M and an undefined payout. The two prior years are no better: FY2024 140.1% of FCF, FY2023 97.8% (inflated by a one-off 57.0M leasehold capex). On the meaningful basis, dividends 126.9M / net income 153.2M = 82.8% - above the 60% ceiling but below the 90% avoid trigger. Fails.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy
rules.note: The regular series can only be reconstructed back to FY2012 because FY2010/FY2011 bundle unseparable specials, so the 13-year data streak runs to the start of the usable window and is window-limited. priorEstimates' 19 years is plausible (implies increases from ~2007) and is used for the screen; either figure passes.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: FCF endpoint is negative (FY2025 -126.4M) so FCF CAGR is undefined; used net income per the rule. NI 76.6M (FY2020) -> 153.2M (FY2025) = 14.88%/yr. Caveat: FY2020 was a depressed base (NI fell 43% that year), and NI has been flat 151-171M since FY2022, so the real recent run-rate is closer to the 4% dividend growth of the last three years.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 ROIC 0.3371 on the prescribed formula (EBIT x (1-t) / (equity + debt - cash)), using the 21% tax fallback since the table carries no FY2021+ pretax. The denominator is tiny and cash-dominated for this asset-light filer, so the series is unstable (>100% in 2016/2017/2019, 290% in 2021); the level is overstated in an absolute sense but the direction - very high returns on a business with no capital intensity - is real.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: Net cash in every one of the 17 years. No debt tag exists anywhere in the filings file, so debt was treated as zero and netDebt = -cash; that is an assumption but directionally certain for an unlevered asset manager.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: CNS is the reference specialist in listed REITs, infrastructure and preferreds: a multi-decade track record in a niche where consultants and allocators screen on 10-year numbers, sticky closed-end-fund and institutional mandates that cannot simply be repriced, and index/benchmark partnerships. It is not a price-competed business, though it is fully exposed to the passive-fee squeeze at the retail end.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.note: Regular dividend rose through COVID and every other year of the window; no cut or hold anywhere FY2013-FY2025. 2008 is outside the XBRL window and cannot be checked. The filed annual DPS series appears to fall in 2013/2015/2019/2020/2022, but those are year-end specials rolling off, not cuts - specials stopped after FY2021 and the regular rate kept rising.

analysis.assessment: CNS is a $3.7B net-cash asset manager yielding 3.45% on its FY2025 regular dividend of $2.48 (3.73% on the $2.68 rate already declared for 2026), with a clean 13-year run of regular increases in the data and probably ~19 in reality once the special-dividend noise before 2012 is set aside. Growth has been 9.7%/yr over five years but only 4.1%/yr over three, and the 2026 raise of 8.1% suggests the high-single-digit era is over, not the mid-teens one. The payout is the problem: $126.9M of dividends against $153.2M of net income is 82.8%, and FCF-based payout is unusable because FY2025 operating cash flow is -$120.4M on consolidated fund/seed purchases - either way there is very little runway to grow the dividend faster than fee earnings. The snowball here is a 3.5% yield compounding at roughly earnings growth, call it 5-8%, with no leverage and no reinvestment need, but it is levered one-for-one to AUM: a 25% drawdown in listed REIT and preferred markets takes fee revenue and the raise with it, and with 83% of earnings already committed there is no cushion to hold the line through it. The one thing most likely to break it is a multi-year outflow cycle out of listed real assets into private or passive vehicles.
analysis.moat: Category-leading listed real-assets specialist - a multi-decade REIT, infrastructure and preferred-securities track record that consultants screen on and that sticky closed-end-fund and institutional mandates are priced off, not a business won on fee level.
strengths: Net cash in all 17 years with no debt tagged anywhere in the filings; balance sheet takes nothing from shareholders
Regular dividend raised every single year FY2013-FY2025 including through COVID (1.44 -> 1.56 -> 1.80), and raised again to 0.67/qtr for 2026
Asset-light: capital intensity is effectively zero (capex 2-12M/yr ex the one-off FY2023 build-out) so almost all earnings are distributable
Yield 3.45% sits high in the usable band without being a distress yield; market cap $3.7B leaves room to compound
risks: Payout 82.8% of net income leaves no cushion; a fee-revenue drawdown forces the dividend to stall
AUM-sensitive single-category franchise - listed REITs, infrastructure and preferreds - so revenue, earnings and the dividend all move with one asset class
Dividend growth decelerating sharply: 9.7% over 5 years but 4.1% over 3 and 8.1% for the 2026 raise
Net income flat at 151-171M since FY2022 while the dividend keeps rising, which is what pushed the payout from 63% to 83% in three years
Structural fee pressure from passive and from the shift of real-asset allocations into private vehicles
analysis.sectorNote: CNS is an asset manager, so rule 4 was run on FCF = CFO - capex as prescribed, but FY2025 CFO is negative (-120.4M) purely because consolidated-fund and seed-investment purchases flow through operating activities - not an operating failure. The FCF payout is therefore meaningless and the payout test was read on net income (82.8%), which is the honest number for a fee-based business. Rule 7's ROIC is also a poor fit: the denominator (equity + debt - cash) is small and cash-dominated for an asset-light filer, producing readings above 100% in several years; the 33.7% FY2025 figure clears the bar on any reasonable variant but should not be read as a precise return. Rule 8's net-cash reading rests on the absence of any debt tag in the filings.

Concrete and durable; it does not compete on price.

analysis.assessment: AWR is a $3.4B regulated California water utility paying a 2.22% trailing yield (2.50% on the post-August-2026 rate of ~$2.182) and compounding the dividend at 8.66%/yr over five years - a clean, believable snowball of roughly 2.2% yield plus high-single-digit growth, backed by 16 straight increases in the data and a research streak of 71 years with no cut in 2020 or 2021. The cover is real but narrow and must be read off earnings, not cash: capex has exceeded operating cash flow in every year since FY2019 (FY2025 CFO $229.7M vs capex $236.8M, FCF -$7.1M), so the dividend is 57.2% of net income and is funded alongside the rate-base build with debt and ATM equity. That funding model is exactly what is straining the other half of the scorecard - net debt/EBITDA has climbed from 1.56x in FY2014 to 3.08x in FY2025, the highest in the series, while ROIC sits at 8.59% in a tight 6-11% band because a regulated utility earns its authorised return and nothing more. Net income grew 8.58%/yr over five years against an 8.66% dividend CAGR, so the payout ratio is creeping up rather than down, leaving no self-financing runway. The thing most likely to break it is a CPUC rate case or cost-of-capital decision that lags inflation and interest expense: with leverage at 3.08x and share count already rising 36.9M to 38.55M since FY2021, an unfavourable return-on-equity ruling would force the growth rate down toward the low-to-mid single digits long before it would force a cut.
analysis.moat: Golden State Water's CPUC-franchised California service territories are legal monopolies over sunk, non-replicable pipe networks, and ASUS holds 50-year sole-source privatisation contracts on US military bases - neither can be bid away by a competitor.
analysis.sectorNote: AWR is a regulated rate-base water utility, so two rules are poor fits and were read accordingly. Rule 4: FCF (CFO - capex) is negative in every year FY2019-FY2025 because capex is the growth engine and is funded with debt and equity by design, so dividends/FCF is meaningless and undefined; payout was assessed against net income (57.2% in FY2025, 44.6%-71.9% across the window) as the rule permits. Rule 6 inherits the same problem - the FY2020 FCF endpoint is negative so a CAGR is undefined - and was therefore run on net income (8.58%/yr) versus the 8.66% dividend CAGR. Rule 7 is not adjusted but should be read in context: a regulated utility earns its CPUC-authorised return, so an 8.6% ROIC is a normal outcome rather than evidence of a weak business - it is nonetheless a real constraint on the compounding rate and is scored as a fail on the stated threshold.

issues.detail: The whole series is CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid, i.e. cash PAID, and FY2025 is internally lumpy (Q1 = 0.34 against 0.30 for Q2/Q3/Q4). The underlying 2025 declared rate is 0.30/qtr = 1.20 annual, and 2026 runs 0.335/qtr. So the 1.24 endpoint carries roughly 0.04 of payment-timing, which inflates g3 and g5 by roughly 1.1pp and 0.7pp respectively versus a declared-rate series. The record discloses the cash-paid basis but does not quantify the effect on the growth figures it publishes.
issues.suggested: Keep 1.24 (it is the filed annual fact and is corroborated at 1.2398), but add to dataQuality that g3/g5 would be ~6.3%/~7.1% on a declared-rate basis (1.20 endpoint), so the growth numbers should not be read to 4 decimal places.

issues.detail: The June-2011 date rests on a single fact (StockholdersEquityNoteStockSplitConversionRatio @ 2011-06-30, 10-Q/A). The raw data is not cleanly consistent with it: the 2010-04-01..2010-06-30 declared fact is already 0.1488 (post-split) in a 10-Q/A, while the 2010-01-01..2010-06-30 fact in the SAME form is 0.2975 - which is a single pre-split quarterly rate sitting on a 180-day duration, i.e. an internally contradictory pair. Those 2010 comparatives are only reconcilable if they were re-filed in 2011 filings, which the extract's form/fp fields cannot confirm. This does NOT change the conclusion (yearsAdjusted=[] holds whether the split was mid-2010 or mid-2011, since sharesBasic is unbroken from 2009 onward), but the note asserts the filing provenance ("the four 2010 quarterly facts in the FY2011/FY2012 10-Ks") as established fact when the file does not carry filing-year metadata.
issues.suggested: Soften the note to: split ratio 2 reported at 2011-06-30; the 2010 quarterly comparatives are already post-split in the data, so FY2009-FY2011 are all restated and zero years require adjustment regardless of the exact effective date.

issues.detail: Arithmetic slip inside the justification text: "FY2010 annual 0.595 = 4 x 0.1488" is false - 4 x 0.1488 = 0.5952. The same claim is repeated in splitAdjustments[0].note. The underlying reasoning is fine (the quarterly facts are rounded to 4dp from 0.14875), but the record states a false identity twice as its primary evidence that FY2010 is already post-split.
issues.suggested: "FY2010 annual 0.595 = 4 x 0.14875, filed rounded to 0.1488 per quarter"

issues.detail: FY2025 capex of 516,991,000 is taken from tagHints.lastVal for PaymentsToAcquireWaterAndWasteWaterSystems. tagHints shows that tag has 18 points (a full 2008-2025 series exists in the filer's XBRL) but the extract exposes only the last value, so the record's one-year FCF is built on an endpoint the file cannot cross-check against any other year. Separately, CapitalExpendituresIncurredButNotYetPaid = 67,831,000 at FY2025 confirms a large accrual/cash timing wedge, on top of the PaymentsToAcquireLifeInsurancePolicies (3,364,000) omission the record already flags. The negative-FCF conclusion survives all of this comfortably (a 67.8m swing does not close a 214.4m gap), so the sign is safe.
issues.suggested: Keep fcf = -214,430,000 and payoutFcf = null, but state in issues that the capex figure is an unverifiable single endpoint and that the full 18-point series should be re-extracted before any FCF trend is published.

issues.detail: Confirmed understated. ShortTermBorrowings is a candidate tag with 17 points (2009-2025) and is excluded because debtCur carries LongTermDebtCurrent. The record flags this, but then still publishes netDebtToEbitda to 4 decimal places and leans on "4.49x, up from 3.14x" in the notes as a headline conclusion. For a filer running commercial paper, the true FY2025 ratio is above 4.4887 by an unknown amount.
issues.suggested: Report netDebtToEbitda as ">=4.49x (excludes ShortTermBorrowings)" rather than a point estimate, or re-extract ShortTermBorrowings and add it to debtCur.

checksRun: 1. Latest regular DPS (FY2025 1.24) vs live.ttmDividend 1.305 -> +5.24% gap, within 10%; fully explained by the 2026 quarterly raise 0.30 -> 0.335 (0.30 + 3 x 0.335 = 1.305 exactly, as of 2026-09-17). No special (regularDividendIfSpecial null, record says hasSpecials false). PASS

2. live.marketCap/price = 2,971,368,755 / 48.05 = 61,839,100 shares; equals coverSharesOutstanding 61,839,101 to the share. vs record latest sharesBasic (FY2025 59,570,000) = +3.8%, well inside 15% and consistent with CWT's continuous equity issuance (sharesBasic rises every year 2009-2025: 41.5M -> 59.6M). No evidence of a missed split. PASS
3. Implied regular yield = 1.24 / 48.05 = 2.58% (2.72% on ttm 1.305). Normal for a regulated water utility; far from the >8% / <0.2% failure bands. PASS

4. g5 = 7.85%/yr for a ~$3.0bn regulated CA water utility (sector Utilities) is plausible and matches the observed rate-base/EPS trajectory; g10 6.35% and gMax 4.75% bracket it sensibly. Independently recomputed: (1.24/0.85)^(1/5)-1 = 7.845%, (1.24/0.67)^(1/10)-1 = 6.349%, (1.24/0.59)^(1/16)-1 = 4.752% - all match the record. PASS

5. Divergences vs priorEstimates: g5 7.85 vs 7 (minor, no flag); streak 16 vs 58 - explicitly explained by streak.windowLimited and the note 'do not read 16 as the true streak'; payoutPctFcf 60 vs null - explained by the capex-extraction gap and negative FY2025 FCF in dataQuality.issues. All divergences are self-disclosed. PASS

6. Streak window: 16 consecutive increases claimed from 17 fiscal years (FY2009-FY2025 = 16 year-over-year transitions, every one an increase). windowLimited=true and firstYearInData=2009 are set. Claim does not exceed the data window. PASS

issues.detail: The series is on a CASH-PAID basis (CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid), while live.ttmDividend is FMP's sum of the last four DECLARED dividends. FY2025 cash-paid 1.24 vs FY2025 declared 4 x 0.30 = 1.20 - a 3.3% basis difference that the record itself traces to a lumpy Q1-2025 cash-paid fact (0.34 + 0.30 x 3). Both bases pass the 10% test against ttm 1.305 (+5.2% and +8.7% respectively), so this is disclosed-and-benign, not a refutation; but any downstream comparison of this series to declared-basis vendor data should note the basis mismatch.
issues.suggested: Keep dps FY2025 = 1.24 (cash-paid, corroborated by divPaid/sharesBasic = 1.2398). Optionally record declaredDps FY2025 = 1.20 and current annualised declared rate = 1.34 (4 x 0.335) alongside, and state the basis explicitly when benchmarking against FMP ttmDividend.

rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: live marketCap 2,971,368,755 at $48.05 (2026-09-17). Comfortably in the ideal band — a small-cap regulated water utility, so incremental rate-base additions still move the needle.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: latest regular annual DPS 1.24 (FY2025 filed, cash-paid basis) / price 48.05 = 2.581%. On the live ttm 1.305 it is 2.72%, and on the current declared rate of 0.335/qtr (1.34 annualised) it is 2.79%. All three readings sit mid-band.

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: g5 = (1.24/0.85)^(1/5)-1 = 7.845%, just under the bar. It is worse than it looks: the FY2025 endpoint is cash-paid and lumpy (Q1 0.34 vs 0.30 for Q2-Q4), so on a declared-rate basis (1.20) g5 is ~7.1%. g3 7.43%, g10 6.35%, gMax 4.75%. Miss, not a near-miss to round up.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.value: 57.6% of net income (FCF payout not meaningful: FY2025 FCF -$214.4M)
rules.note: SECTOR CARVE-OUT APPLIED: regulated utility with FCF <= 0 because of rate-base capex, so assessed against net income per the rule. FY2025 dividends 73,853,000 / net income 128,211,000 = 57.6%, inside 20-60% but with only ~2pp of headroom. FY2025 CFO 302.6M less capex 517.0M = -214.4M, so the dividend is funded by debt and equity issuance, not internally generated cash. FY2023 payoutNi was 113.7% on a depressed earnings year — the metric is volatile.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy, short enough to still be fast
rules.note: The XBRL window starts FY2009 and shows 16 straight increases with no hold or cut, so the data streak is window-limited. Prior research streak of 58 years is plausible and consistent (CWT is a long-standing Dividend King). Using 58: it clears the 10-year floor decisively but breaks the 30-year ceiling, which is exactly the failure mode this rule screens for — a very mature policy whose growth has already decelerated to single digits (gMax 4.75%).

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.value: 5-yr NI CAGR 5.78% vs DPS CAGR 7.85% (NI substituted)
rules.note: FCF SUBSTITUTED WITH NET INCOME: capex is recoverable for FY2025 only, so fcfGrowth5 is null and the FY2020 FCF endpoint does not exist. Net income 96,831,000 (FY2020) -> 128,211,000 (FY2025) = 5.78%/yr, a 2.07pp shortfall against dividend growth — the payout ratio has been rising as a result (43.1% in FY2020 to 57.6% in FY2025). On a 10-year view NI CAGR is 11.0% (45.0M FY2015 -> 128.2M FY2025), so the shortfall is recent, driven by the weak FY2023 (51.9M) and the FY2024 191M spike that flatters the base year comparison in the other direction.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.value: n/a for FY2025 (equity missing); 7.31% FY2020, the highest in 12 computable years
rules.note: Equity drops out of the extract from FY2021, so ROIC is null for FY2021-FY2025. The rule is still assessable on history: every one of the 12 computable years (FY2009-FY2020) sits between 3.97% and 7.31%, never remotely near 12%. This is structural, not a data artifact — a regulated utility earns an allowed return on rate base (roughly 9-10% on equity, less after leverage and tax), so ROIC above 12% is not achievable by design.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: FY2025 net debt 1,422,418,000 / EBITDA 316,892,000 = 4.4887x, up sharply from 3.14x in FY2024 on a ~367M increase in long-term debt. And it is understated: ShortTermBorrowings (commercial paper) is excluded from the net-debt build, so the true figure is above 4.49x. Only FY2017 (2.35x) has ever cleared 2.5x in the 17-year window. Crosses the >4x avoid trigger.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.threshold: concrete durable mechanism, not price competition
rules.note: CWT holds state-granted exclusive franchises to supply water in defined California, Washington, New Mexico, Hawaii and Texas territories; no competitor can lay a duplicate distribution network into a served household, and pricing is set by regulators rather than by rivalry. The moat is real, but it is a moat on a return that regulators cap — it protects the revenue, not the ROIC.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.threshold: no cut in FY2020/FY2021; any cut or suspension in window fails
rules.note: Sixteen consecutive annual increases FY2010-FY2025, zero holds, zero cuts, no COVID pause, no special dividends. 2008 is outside the XBRL window and cannot be checked from this data. divPaid/sharesBasic corroborates the filed DPS to within 0.33% in every year, so the increase record is not an artifact of tagging.

analysis.sectorNote: CWT is a regulated water utility, so three rules are poor fits and were read accordingly. Rule 4 was assessed against net income (57.6%) rather than FCF, because FY2025 FCF is -$214.4M by design: a rate-base utility raises debt and equity to fund capex and recovers it through rates over decades, so negative FCF is the business model, not distress — but it does mean the dividend is not covered by internally generated cash. Rule 6 likewise falls back to net income. Rule 7 (ROIC > 12%) is structurally unreachable for any regulated utility, since the allowed return is set by commissions; the 3.97-7.31% range observed is normal for the sector rather than evidence of a bad business. Rule 8 is the one where the sector excuse does NOT hold — utilities do run 3-4x leverage routinely, but 4.49x and rising, with commercial paper excluded, is high even against utility peers and it is what funds the dividend.
analysis.assessment: CWT offers a 2.58% starting yield on the FY2025 regular DPS of $1.24 (2.79% on the current $0.335 quarterly declared rate) growing at 7.85%/yr over five years — a ~10.4% snowball before multiple change, which is respectable but not the 8%+ growth this screen demands, and on a declared-rate basis growth is closer to 7.1%. The runway is thinner than the headline: net income grew only 5.78%/yr over the same five years against 7.85% dividend growth, pushing the payout from 43.1% of earnings in FY2020 to 57.6% in FY2025, so each further raise now has to come out of a shrinking cushion. There is no FCF cushion at all — FY2025 CFO of $302.6M against $517.0M of rate-base capex gives -$214.4M of free cash flow, meaning every dollar of the $73.9M dividend is effectively financed, and net debt/EBITDA has jumped from 3.14x to at least 4.49x in one year on ~$367M of new long-term debt. The thing most likely to break it is a California rate case that comes in below the requested return while the capital programme keeps running: that is exactly the FY2023 pattern (net income $51.9M, payout 113.7% of earnings, leverage 5.06x), and a repeat with leverage already at 4.5x forces the choice between equity issuance that dilutes the 3.8%-a-year share growth further and slowing the dividend to a token 2-3% raise. A 58-year increase record and an exclusive regulated franchise make an outright cut unlikely; the realistic downside is a dividend that quietly decelerates toward 3-4% growth, which is not the compounder this screen is looking for.
analysis.moat: Regulated water across five states under exclusive state-granted service territories no competitor can duplicate, with rate base growing alongside capital spend — but regulators cap the return, so the moat protects revenue, not ROIC.
strengths: 58-year dividend increase record (16 confirmed in the FY2009-FY2025 XBRL window) with zero holds, zero cuts, no COVID pause and no special dividends; divPaid/sharesBasic corroborates the filed DPS to within 0.33% every single year.
Exclusive regulated service territories in CA, WA, NM, HI and TX — a genuine structural monopoly on the served household.
$2.97B market cap, deep in the ideal <$5B band; rate-base additions are still material relative to the base.
Starting yield of 2.58% sits mid-band and is well clear of the distress zone; FY2025 payout of 57.6% of earnings is still inside the 20-60% window.
risks: Net debt/EBITDA of at least 4.49x (understated — excludes commercial paper) after a ~$367M one-year increase in long-term debt; crosses the >4x avoid trigger and was 5.06x as recently as FY2023.
FY2025 FCF is -$214.4M (CFO $302.6M less capex $517.0M): the dividend is funded by external capital, not internally generated cash.
Earnings growth (5-yr NI CAGR 5.78%) is running 2.07pp behind dividend growth (7.85%), so the payout ratio is on a rising path — 43.1% in FY2020 to 57.6% in FY2025.
Earnings are rate-case-volatile: FY2023 net income of $51.9M put payout at 113.7%; a single adverse California decision repeats that with leverage now much higher.
Persistent equity issuance — basic shares up from 41.5M (FY2009) to 59.6M (FY2025), ~3.8% a year recently — dilutes per-share growth and is the funding mechanism the capex plan depends on.
ROIC has never exceeded 7.31% in twelve computable years and is structurally capped by regulators; it is also unmeasurable for FY2021-FY2025 because equity is missing from the extract.

screenFields.streakSource: research; data confirms 16 years (FY2009-FY2025 window-limited, no holds or cuts)
screenFields.payoutBasis: percent of net income (regulated utility with FY2025 FCF of -$214.4M; FCF payout not computable or meaningful)

estimateCorrections.why: Basis change, not a small revision. The prior 60% implied a positive, covered FCF payout; FY2025 FCF is actually -$214.4M (CFO $302.6M less rate-base capex $517.0M), so an FCF payout ratio does not exist for CWT. The 57.6% now shown is dividends/net income, the sector-appropriate substitute, and the screen must label it as such — otherwise a reader sees '57.6% of FCF' and concludes coverage that is not there.
Not previously tracked. At >=4.49x (understated, excludes commercial paper) this is the single metric that drives the 'avoid' verdict, up from 3.14x in FY2024, and it belongs on the screen.

Not previously tracked and not computable for FY2021-FY2025 because equity drops out of the extract. Recorded as null rather than carried forward: the last computable year (FY2020) was 7.31%, and no year in twelve exceeded that, so any ROIC-based filter should treat CWT as structurally sub-12%.

Below the 3pp materiality bar (0.85pp) so not a correction in the strict sense, but logged because the direction is misleading: the 7.85% rests on a cash-paid FY2025 endpoint of 1.24 against a declared rate of 1.20, and on a declared basis g5 is ~7.1% — i.e. the prior estimate of 7 was closer to the economic truth than the derived figure.

No change. The data streak of 16 is window-limited (XBRL begins FY2009) and the prior research figure of 58 is plausible and internally consistent with 16 unbroken increases at the front of the window, so the research figure is retained and the data confirmation is recorded alongside it.

stocks.m: Exclusive state-granted gas and electric distribution franchises in fast-growing Delmarva and Florida territories - a legal monopoly on the pipes and wires with an allowed regulated return, where customer growth arrives with population rather than being won from anyone.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (FY duration ~364 days, 10-K) used for every year except FY2020. FY2009-FY2011 divided by 1.5 for the September 2013 3-for-2 split (FY2012 onward were already filed on the post-split basis). FY2020's filed annual fact (1.585) is an XBRL error - it duplicates FY2019 - so FY2020 was rebuilt from the quarterly rate facts: 0.405 (Q1) + 0.44 + 0.44 + 0.44 = 1.725, corroborated by declared Dividends/shares = 1.7417 and by the FY2021 Q1 rate of 0.44. Every year cross-checked against both PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock/sharesBasic and the declared 'Dividends' tag/sharesBasic.

splitAdjustments.note: 3-for-2 split effective September 2013. Evidence for the date: the quarterly declared rate fell from 0.385 (Q2 2013) to 0.257 (Q3 2013), a factor of 1.4981, and FY2013's filed annual 1.0133 = 0.365/1.5 + 0.385/1.5 + 0.257 + 0.257. Evidence for WHICH years are on the old basis: sharesBasic steps from 9,555,799 (FY2011) to 14,379,216 (FY2012), a 1.505x jump, and the raw filed DPS steps 1.365 (FY2011) -> 0.96 (FY2012), so FY2012 is already post-split while FY2011 is not. FY2012 and FY2013 therefore needed NO adjustment; only FY2009-FY2011 were divided by 1.5 and their shares multiplied by 1.5. This is one year narrower than the textbook two-year restatement window would predict - the FY2013 10-K did restate FY2011 on its income statement, but the companyfacts extract kept the original pre-split FY2011 fact. The adjusted series 0.8333 / 0.8700 / 0.9100 / 0.9600 is smooth with ~0.04/yr steps, which no other choice produces.

specials.note: No special dividends found. The filed DPS sits 3.7-13.0% ABOVE PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock/sharesBasic in every single year, which is a uniform structural gap (DRIP shares are issued rather than paid in cash, plus declared-vs-paid timing), not a special in any one year. Declared-tag cross-check available FY2009-FY2012 (DividendsCommonStockCash) and FY2015-FY2025 (Dividends), matching filed DPS to within 0.0-1.2% except FY2009 +2.6% and FY2023 +3.9%; FY2013 and FY2014 have no declared-dividend fact and rest on the filed DPS alone. Live ttmDividend 2.84 = Q4-2025 0.685 + Q1-2026 0.685 + Q2-2026 0.735 + Q3-2026 0.735, where the Q3-2026 rate is inferred from the Q2-2026 rate holding (the filed Q3-2026 fact is a zero placeholder); the +5.4% gap to FY2025 DPS is fully explained by the Q2-2026 raise. Live regularDividendIfSpecial is null.

issues: FY2020 filed annual DPS is wrong in the source data. CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared for 2020-01-01..2020-12-31 (10-K) is 1.585, identical to FY2019. The FY2020 quarterly rate facts are 0.405 / 0.44 / 0.44, and the FY2021 Q1 rate is 0.44, so Q4 2020 was 0.44 and the declared total is 1.725. The 10-Q/A 9M YTD fact of 1.285 refutes the filed annual: 1.585 would force a Q4 rate of 0.30, below the Q1 rate of 0.405. JUDGEMENT CALL: I overrode the filed annual value with 1.725 (basis 'summed-quarters'). Using the filed 1.585 would make FY2020 a flat year and cut the streak from 16 to 5.

SPLIT SCOPE JUDGEMENT CALL: the September 2013 3-for-2 split required adjusting only FY2009, FY2010 and FY2011 (3 years), not FY2012 or FY2013. That is one year narrower than the 'split year plus two prior years already restated' rule predicts. Evidence: sharesBasic jumps 9,555,799 -> 14,379,216 between FY2011 and FY2012 (1.505x), raw filed DPS steps 1.365 -> 0.96, and the FY2013 quarterly reconciliation 0.365/1.5 + 0.385/1.5 + 0.257 + 0.257 = 1.0133. Likely cause: the companyfacts extract kept the ORIGINAL FY2011 10-K fact rather than the FY2013 10-K restated comparative.

splitFacts is an empty array - there is no split-ratio fact in the data, so the 1.5 ratio and the timing were inferred from the Q2->Q3 2013 quarterly rate step (0.385 -> 0.257 = /1.4981) and the FY2013 annual reconciliation. Only the QUARTER is evidenced; the exact date 2013-09-09 in splitAdjustments is an inference, not a sourced value.

netDebt excludes ShortTermBorrowings, a 16-point debtCur candidate (2010-12-31 to 2025-12-31) that was not joined into the table. For a rate-base utility running commercial paper this is material: the reported netDebtToEbitda of 4.59x (FY2025) is a FLOOR, not the full figure, and the same understatement applies to every year from FY2010 on.

divPaid in fin uses the primary tag PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock, which is CASH dividends paid and excludes shares issued under the dividend reinvestment plan. It runs BELOW declared DPS x sharesBasic in EVERY year: 2009 -13.0%, 2010 -10.9%, 2011 -10.6%, 2012 -10.6%, 2013 -10.5%, 2014 -10.5%, 2015 -6.8%, 2016 -6.6%, 2017 -4.7%, 2018 -6.2%, 2019 -5.0%, 2020 -5.8%, 2021 -4.5%, 2022 -4.7%, 2023 -5.5%, 2024 -3.9%, 2025 -3.7%. The gap is structural DRIP, not a special dividend. Consequence: every payoutFcf and payoutNi here understates the declared payout by roughly 4%; on a declared basis FY2025 payoutNi would be 0.4549 rather than 0.4326.

Declared-tag coverage is incomplete: the Dividends series starts at 2015-12-31 and DividendsCommonStockCash ends at 2012-12-31, so FY2013 and FY2014 have NO declared-dividend fact and cannot be cross-checked by that route - exactly two of the years where the divPaid/shares gap is widest (-10.5%).

FY2009 ROIC, netDebt and netDebtToEbitda are null: the table has no debtLT and no debtCur for 2009-12-31 (both LongTermDebtAndCapitalLeaseObligations and LongTermDebtCurrent start at 2010-12-31), so invested capital and net debt cannot be built.

FY2024 and FY2025 have no pretax value in the table - the primary pretax tag stops at 2023-12-31 and the alternate tag's series is empty. Rather than use the 21% fallback I derived pretax as netIncome + tax (FY2024 161,800k, eff rate 26.70%; FY2025 193,000k, eff rate 27.31%). The proxy validates on FY2023 (115,300k vs filed 115,290k, 0.01% off) and FY2021 (exact). The flat 21% fallback would instead give FY2024 ROIC 0.0669 and FY2025 0.0633.

Capex: two competing tags cover 2022-2025. I used PaymentsToAcquirePropertyPlantAndEquipment (17 points, full window) and named it in capexTag. PaymentsToAcquireProductiveAssets gives 1,138,000,000 for FY2023, roughly 6x the PP&E figure, because it bundles the Florida City Gas acquisition - rejected as not capex. The two also differ by 21.8m in FY2025 (448.6 vs 470.4) and 12.5m in FY2022; FCF would be that much lower on the alternate tag.

FCF is negative in 11 of 17 years (FY2012-FY2021, FY2024, FY2025) because this is a rate-base utility funding a capex program far above CFO, so payoutFcf is null for those years by rule. The two positive-FCF recent years give payoutFcf of 1.15 (FY2022) and 2.68 (FY2023): the dividend is not covered by free cash flow on any recent measure. priorEstimates payoutPctFcf = 40 is unsupported by this data and was discarded.
fcfGrowth5 is null: both endpoints are negative FCF (FY2020 -6,595k, FY2025 -214,900k), so a CAGR is undefined.

Sign-convention problem in the source: FY2020 buybacks -22,627,000, FY2021 -15,851,000, FY2022 -4,534,000 and the ProceedsFromRepurchaseOfEquity hint (-721,000) are all sign-flipped, i.e. net share issuance booked under repurchase tags. Not used in any computation here, but flagged.

Balance-sheet duplication in the source: FY2012 carries the identical cash (3,361,000) and debtCur (8,196,000) as FY2011, and FY2012 debtLT differs from FY2011 by only 182k. FY2012 netDebt and netDebtToEbitda are therefore slightly suspect, though the magnitudes are plausible.

FY2009 sharesBasic (10,969,980 split-adjusted) is a weighted average depressed by the October 2009 Florida Public Utilities merger, which issued a large share block late in the year; revenue also jumps 59% into FY2010 for the same reason. FY2009 payout and per-share cross-checks are the least reliable in the window.

priorEstimates (growth5y 9, streak 21, payoutPctFcf 40) were ignored as instructed. The 5-year growth guess happens to land near my computed 9.33, but the streak of 21 cannot be verified: the data window starts at FY2009, so consecutiveIncreasesInData is capped at 16 and windowLimited is true.

The last dpsAllFacts entry (2026-07-01..2026-09-30, val 0, form 10-Q, fp Q1) is a zero-valued placeholder with a mislabelled fiscal period and was excluded. Several other quarterly facts carry wrong fp labels (FY2018 Q1 tagged 'Q2', FY2019 Q1 tagged 'Q3', FY2019 Q2 tagged 'Q3', FY2025 Q3 tagged 'Q1'), so I aligned quarters by start/end dates and duration, never by the fp field.

FY2026 is partially observable (Q1 0.685, Q2 0.735, H1 1.42) but incomplete, so it is excluded from dps and fin. The implied FY2026 declared total is 0.685 + 0.735x3 = 2.89 if the usual raise-in-Q2 pattern holds.

normalised.notes: CPK is a December-FYE gas/electric utility with 17 fiscal years of data (FY2009-FY2025). Regular DPS on today's share basis runs 0.8333 (FY2009) to 2.695 (FY2025), a 7.61%/yr CAGR over 16 years that has ACCELERATED rather than decayed: 9.06%/yr over 10 years, 9.33% over 5, 8.93% over 3. Sixteen consecutive years of increases within the window, no cut, no hold, no special dividend, and no cut in 2020 or 2021 - the apparent FY2020 flat line is an XBRL duplication of the FY2019 value, not a real hold. Two normalisations carry the record: (1) the September 2013 3-for-2 split, adjusted for FY2009-FY2011 ONLY, since FY2012 onward were already filed post-split; (2) FY2020 DPS rebuilt from quarterly rates as 1.725. The financial picture behind the dividend has deteriorated markedly since the FY2023 Florida City Gas acquisition: net debt/EBITDA went from 2.90x (FY2022) to 5.64x (FY2023) and sits at 4.59x; ROIC fell from a 9-10% band in FY2010-FY2017 to 5.83% in FY2025; and FCF is deeply negative (-214.9m in FY2025, a -23.1% FCF margin) on a capex program now 1.9x CFO. Payout on net income is a comfortable 43%, but at the free-cash-flow level the dividend is entirely debt- and equity-funded. Confidence is medium rather than high because FY2013/FY2014 have no second-source declared-dividend fact and because netDebt omits ShortTermBorrowings; the FY2020 override and the split window are themselves well evidenced.

analysis.assessment: CPK is the shape of a good snowball wrapped around a balance sheet that is no longer safe: a $3.1bn regulated gas/electric utility yielding 2.08% on the FY2025 declared DPS of $2.695 (2.27% on the current $2.94 run-rate), compounding the dividend at 9.33%/yr over five years with 16 straight increases in the data and no cut in 2020 or 2021. Share count went from 16.7m (FY2020) to 23.4m (FY2025), a 40% dilution, which is how the 14.4% net income growth was paid for. The thing most likely to break it is not a dividend cut but the funding mix: if rates stay high or a Florida or Delaware rate case comes in short of the allowed return, the capex program gets funded with more equity at a lower price, and the 9%/yr dividend growth has to slow to whatever the regulator lets earnings do.

rules.name: Small enough to grow
rules.note: Live marketCap 1,062,329,885 at $164.37 (2026-09-17). Micro/small-cap, deep inside the ideal band; ~6.5M shares outstanding after a 37% reduction from 10.6M in FY2009.

rules.name: Starting yield in the usable band
rules.note: Regular annual DPS on the current basis is 2.28 (4 x the 0.57 quarterly rate); 2.28/164.37 = 1.39%. On the filed FY2025 DPS of 2.04 the yield is 1.24%. No special dividends, so this is a clean regular yield. Misses the 1.5% floor by 11bp - the entry yield is the weak link, because management routes far more cash to buybacks (47.1M in FY2025) than to dividends (13.8M).

rules.name: Dividend growth above 8%/yr
rules.note: 5-yr DPS CAGR FY2020 0.95 -> FY2025 2.04 = 16.51%; 3-yr is 16.51% and the FY2017-FY2025 rate off the first full year is 16.77%. Strong band. If the disputed FY2022 quarterly reading (1.34) were used instead of the filed 1.29, the 3-yr CAGR would be 14.98% - still strong. Nine straight Q4 raises, and the 0.49 -> 0.57 raise (+16.3%) already declared keeps the pace.

rules.name: Payout with room left
rules.note: FY2025 dividends 13.831M / FCF 18.556M = 74.5%, above the 60% ceiling. This is a cash-conversion artefact, not a payout decision: FY2025 CFO collapsed to 22.4M against 54.8M of net income on working-capital/bonus timing. On net income the payout is 25.3%, and on 3-yr average FCF ((57.7+33.1+18.6)/3 = 36.5M) it is 37.9% - both comfortably inside the band. Marked fail on the literal rule; the honest read is that the structural payout is ~25-38% with real room.

rules.name: Streak long enough to prove policy
rules.note: Nine consecutive increases, FY2017 through FY2025, off a dividend initiated in fiscal 2016 at 0.14/quarter. NOT window-limited: the XBRL window starts FY2009 and strictly contains the initiation year, so the prior research estimate of 10 cannot be layered on - the tenth increase does not exist yet. The already-declared 0.57 rate makes FY2026 the tenth, so this rule flips to pass within a year. Fails now on a technicality, but for the good reason that the policy is young rather than broken.

rules.name: Earnings growing at least as fast as the dividend
rules.note: On the literal FCF test this fails badly: FCF went 37.569M (FY2020) -> 18.556M (FY2025) = -13.16%/yr. But FCF is plainly erratic here (73.1M in FY2021, 21.3M in FY2022, 57.7M in FY2023, 18.6M in FY2025) on a business with no real capital intensity, so per the rule's carve-out I used net income: 24.507M -> 54.782M = 17.45%/yr, just ahead of the 16.51% dividend CAGR. Revenue 508.4M -> 751.6M and EBITDA 47.6M -> 97.3M corroborate. Pass on net income, stated as such.

rules.name: High return on invested capital
rules.note: FY2025 NOPAT 83.124M x (1 - 28.46%) = 59.5M over equity 213.6M less cash 18.2M = 30.4%. Debt is absent from the source, so the denominator omits borrowings and this is a ceiling; FY2025 interest of 4.659M at a ~6% cost implies roughly 75-80M of debt, which puts the true figure near 22%. Either number clears the 15% strong bar comfortably, and the five-year trend (15.5% -> 30.6% -> 24.3% -> 25.4% -> 26.9% -> 30.4%) is consistent. An asset-light consultancy whose capital is people, so high ROIC is structurally expected.

rules.name: Balance sheet not competing with you
rules.note: Not assessable: the source has no debt family at all (no DebtCurrent, LongTermDebt, LongTermDebtNoncurrent or LineOfCredit), so netDebt is null for all 17 years and zero was correctly not substituted. Indirect bounding: interest of 4.659M implies ~75-80M drawn, against cash of 18.2M and EBITDA of 97.3M, so indicative net debt/EBITDA is roughly 0.6x - well clear of 2.5x. Treated as null rather than a pass because the figure is inferred, not filed.

rules.name: Why competitors cannot take the business
rules.note: CRAI sells the testimony and reports of named PhD economists whose credibility has been accepted by courts, antitrust agencies and regulators; law firms retain the individual expert and the case team around them, and a challenger cannot manufacture a Daubert-survivable track record or the conflict-cleared roster that follows from it. Pricing is on billable rates that rise with that reputation, not bid down - revenue grew 324.8M -> 751.6M (FY2016-FY2025) while headcount economics held. The honest weakness is that the franchise walks out of the door in people's heads: expert teams do defect, which is the real competitive risk rather than price.

rules.name: Management treats the dividend as a promise
rules.note: Through COVID the dividend rose 14.5% in FY2020 and 14.7% in FY2021, with no hold or suspension anywhere in the FY2016-FY2025 data. 2008 is outside the XBRL window and, more to the point, CRAI paid no dividend at all before fiscal 2016, so there is no earlier cut to find. Buybacks are treated as the flexible lever and the dividend as the fixed one, which is the right ordering.

analysis.assessment: CRAI is a $1.06B consultancy compounding the dividend at 16.5%/yr off a nine-year streak, but the snowball starts cold: 2.28 annualised on a $164.37 price is a 1.39% yield, below the usable floor, because management spends roughly 3.4x more on buybacks (47.1M in FY2025) than on dividends (13.8M). The runway is genuinely long - 25.3% of net income and ~38% of three-year average FCF - so the headline 74.5% FY2025 FCF payout is a cash-conversion artefact of a 22.4M CFO against 54.8M of net income, not a stretched policy. Earnings are keeping up (net income 17.45%/yr vs DPS 16.51%/yr, revenue 508M -> 752M over five years) on a 30.4% reported ROIC that is closer to ~22% once the ~75-80M of inferred borrowings are added back, and leverage looks near 0.6x EBITDA although no debt is actually filed. At this yield you are buying growth, not income: a 15-year hold at mid-teens growth gets you to a 10-12% yield on cost, and nothing gets there faster. The thing most likely to break it is the revenue engine, not the balance sheet - billings track antitrust, litigation and regulatory activity, so a quiet enforcement cycle or the defection of a few senior expert teams hits revenue and the bonus-heavy cost base at once, and CFO has already shown it can halve in a year.
analysis.moat: CRA sells named PhD economists whose testimony courts and antitrust agencies have already accepted - a Daubert-survivable, conflict-cleared expert roster that a competitor cannot assemble on demand, which is why the work is retained at rising rates rather than bid on price.
strengths: 16.51% 5-yr DPS CAGR with nine straight Q4 raises and a tenth (0.49 -> 0.57, +16.3%) already declared.
Payout is genuinely low on the durable denominators: 25.3% of net income, ~37.9% of 3-yr average FCF.
ROIC of 30.4% reported / ~22% debt-adjusted on an asset-light people business; capex is 0.5-2.4% of revenue in most years.
Net income compounding at 17.45%/yr, slightly ahead of the dividend, with revenue 324.8M -> 751.6M since FY2016.
Aggressive buyback shrinking the share count 10.6M -> 6.5M, which mechanically amplifies per-share dividend growth.
Dividend raised straight through FY2020 and FY2021 with no hold or cut anywhere in the window.
risks: 1.39% entry yield fails the usable band; the snowball needs ~5 more years of mid-teens growth just to reach a 2.5% yield on cost.

Cash conversion is erratic - CFO was 22.4M against 54.8M of net income in FY2025 and 25.1M against 43.6M in FY2022; a third weak year would make the FCF payout structural rather than a timing artefact.
No debt is filed anywhere in the source, so leverage is unverifiable; interest rising from 0.24M (FY2015) to 4.659M (FY2025) shows borrowings have grown alongside the buyback.
Revenue is tied to litigation, antitrust and regulatory activity - a quieter enforcement cycle hits billings directly.
The moat is human: senior expert teams can and do leave, taking client relationships with them.
Streak is only 9 years, so the dividend policy is not yet proven across a full cycle (no dividend existed in 2008-09).
analysis.sectorNote: Standard industrial/professional-services model, so the rules mostly fit as written. Two exceptions: rule 4 was read on net income (25.3%) and 3-yr average FCF (37.9%) alongside the failing single-year FCF figure (74.5%), because a people business with ~1% capex intensity has FCF that swings entirely on bonus and receivable timing; and rule 8 is marked null rather than passed because the filer's debt is absent from the XBRL source, with an interest-implied ~0.6x noted as indicative only.

normalised.dpsMethod: Filed annual CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared (~364-365 day FY duration, 10-K) for every year FY2009-FY2025. splitAdjustments.note: 2-for-1 split (StockholdersEquityNoteStockSplitConversionRatio = 2, declared 2012-01-27, effected 2012-03-23, i.e. inside FY2012). Evidence for adjusting exactly one year: (i) sharesBasic steps from 77,967,141 (FY2009) to 155,697,056 (FY2010), a clean 2x step marking the basis boundary; (ii) FY2009 divPaid/shares = 0.2255 which on the OLD basis is 0.4510, self-consistent with its filed DPS of 0.46 (+2.0%), so FY2009 is pre-split; (iii) FY2010 divPaid/shares = 0.2328 is self-consistent with filed 0.24 (+3.1%) on the NEW basis, so FY2010 is already restated. This matches the restatement window exactly: the FY2012 10-K restated FY2012, FY2011 and FY2010; FY2009 last appeared in the FY2011 10-K (filed Sept 2011, pre-split). Adjustments applied: DPS 0.46 -> 0.23; sharesBasic 77,967,141 -> 155,934,282. No later split: coverSharesOutstanding 115,911,056 (2026-05-21) vs FY2025 basic 118,700,000 is buyback shrinkage.

specials.note: No special dividend found. Filed annual DPS never exceeds divPaid/weighted-basic-shares by more than ~10.6% (FY2013), and that gap is fully explained by declaration-vs-payment timing during a rapid raise: FY2013 declared quarters 0.09+0.10+0.13+0.13 = 0.45, while CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid for the same quarters = 0.09+0.09+0.10+0.13 = 0.41, matching the 0.4068 implied by cash paid / shares. No year shows a DPS spike above trend and PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock rises smoothly every year.

issues: SPLIT (key judgement): FY2009 is the ONLY year adjusted for the 2-for-1 split effected 2012-03-23 (DPS 0.46 -> 0.23; sharesBasic 77,967,141 -> 155,934,282). FY2010, FY2011 and FY2012 were already restated post-split by the FY2012 10-K and were deliberately NOT divided. Evidence: sharesBasic steps exactly 2x between FY2009 (77.97M) and FY2010 (155.70M); divPaid/shares is self-consistent with the filed DPS inside each basis (FY2009 0.4510 vs 0.46 on the old basis; FY2010 0.2328 vs 0.24 on the new basis). Exactly one year adjusted, consistent with the three-year restatement window of a FY2012 split.
SPLIT consequence: had FY2009 been left unadjusted the series would read 0.46 -> 0.24, a false 48% cut in FY2010 and a broken streak. After adjustment the series rises every single year.

CFO GAP: FY2014 and FY2015 are absent from NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivities (15 points for 17 years). Substituted NetCashProvidedByUsedInOperatingActivitiesContinuingOperations: FY2014 = 317,800,000, FY2015 = 212,800,000. That tag matches the primary exactly for FY2012/FY2013 but differs for FY2016 (286.1M vs 291.3M) and FY2017 (310.3M vs 317.8M), so FY2014/FY2015 CFO, FCF and payoutFcf may be understated by roughly 1-2%.

FY2009 netDebt, netDebtToEbitda and roic are null: LongTermDebt and ShortTermBorrowings have no FY2009 fact (both series start 2010-07-31). Debt was not assumed to be zero, since DCI carried ~$312M of total debt at FY2010; assuming zero would have inflated FY2009 ROIC.

Revenue is null for FY2009-FY2016. RevenueFromContractWithCustomerIncludingAssessedTax starts 2017-07-31, and the per-year join table carries no revenue before FY2017. The legacy Revenues tag is listed as a candidate for 2016-2019 but was not joined into the table, so no FY2016 value was derivable.

CROSS-CHECK DISAGREEMENTS beyond ~5%: FY2013 filed DPS 0.45 vs divPaid/shares 0.4068 (+10.6%); FY2014 0.61 vs 0.5707 (+6.9%); FY2012 0.335 vs 0.3173 (+5.6%); FY2011 0.28 vs 0.2656 (+5.4%). All four fall in the 2011-2014 window when DCI was raising the dividend 15-20% a year, so declared ran ahead of cash paid. Confirmed as timing rather than specials via CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid. The other 13 years agree within 3.1%.

dpsAllFacts quarterly durations are partly unreliable, which is why quarterly summation was rejected in favour of the filed annual tag: the four CommonStockDividendsPerShareCashPaid facts dated to FY2014 quarters (0.165, 0.165, 0.165, 0.17) sum to 0.665, exactly the filed FY2015 annual CashPaid value, so they appear mis-dated one year early. The FY2014 cumulative facts in the same set (0.27 at Q2, 0.41 at Q3) are instead consistent with the 0.5707 implied by divPaid/shares.

dpsAllFacts contains MIXED split bases inside FY2010/FY2011: quarterly declared and paid rates for those years (0.115, 0.12, 0.13, 0.15) are pre-split while the annual values for the same fiscal years (0.24, 0.28) are post-split restated. FY2010 quarterly CashPaid sums to 0.47 = 2 x 0.235. A second reason quarterly summation was not used.

Two corrupt facts ignored: CommonStockDividendsPerShareDeclared = 380 for periods 2018-08-01/2019-01-31 and 2018-11-01/2019-01-31 (clearly 0.38 with a scale error). Also several zero-valued quarterly declared facts (FY2014 Q1 and Q3, FY2023 Q3, FY2024 Q3, FY2025 Q3, FY2026 Q3) reflecting quarters containing no declaration date.

FY2018 ROIC of 15.6% is depressed by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act: effective tax rate = 183.3/363.6 = 50.4% against a 23-29% norm. On a normalised ~25% rate FY2018 ROIC would be roughly 23.6%. The same charge drags FY2018 payoutNi to 52.5%.

STREAK IS WINDOW-LIMITED: 16 consecutive fiscal years of strictly rising regular DPS (FY2010 through FY2025) is the full extent of the data, which begins at FY2009. DCI's real increase record extends before FY2009, so the true streak is longer than 16 but is not derivable from these facts. No cut and no hold anywhere in the window, including FY2020 and FY2021.

priorEstimates were discarded as instructed and all three were materially off: growth5y guessed 9% vs computed 6.30%; payoutPctFcf guessed 30% vs computed 38.8%; streak guessed 30 vs 16 measurable in this window (30 may be true in reality but is not derivable here).
divPaid uses PaymentsOfDividendsCommonStock. The alternative DividendsCommonStockCash tag has sign inversions (negative for FY2010-FY2012) and values 1-3% higher throughout, so it was rejected.
FY2015 payoutFcf of 76.6% and FY2022 of 65.8% are single-year spikes caused by weak operating cash flow (CFO 212.8M and 252.8M), not dividend policy: DPS rose only 3.0% and 4.7% in those years.

The raw file exposes no series for debtCur/debtLT, so the size of the gap is not derivable here. Not a block: the record followed the stated formula with the primary tags, but this is unflagged in dataQuality.

The substituted ContinuingOperations tag runs LOWER than the primary where both exist (FY2016 286.1M vs 291.3M; FY2017 310.3M vs 317.8M).
